stem:
A 38-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV attends his sexual health clinic appointment for review of staging results. He is asymptomatic with no constitutional symptoms, no respiratory symptoms, and no oral candidiasis. His CD4 count is 250 cells/microlitre and HIV viral load 86,000 copies/mL. He has no other medical conditions, no sulfa allergy, and no current medications. He is keen to start antiretroviral therapy and asks about additional prophylaxis given his low CD4 count.

The clinic registrar has called you to clarify the prophylaxis plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 120/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush; lymphadenopathy minimal in cervical chains; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: CD4 250 cells/microlitre; HIV RNA 86,000 copies/mL; Toxoplasma IgG positive; cryptococcal antigen negative; chest X-ray clear; LFTs and renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylaxis to commence?

options.text: Azithromycin 1200 mg orally once weekly to prevent Mycobacterium avium complex infection.
Fluconazole 400 mg orally once weekly to prevent invasive cryptococcal meningitis disease.
Pyrimethamine 50 mg plus sulfadiazine 1 g daily for toxoplasmosis prophylaxis given positive IgG.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally once daily for Pneumocystis prophylaxis.
Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 6 months as latent tuberculosis prophylaxis regardless of QFT result.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department from her aged care facility with 24 hours of progressive confusion, fever, and reduced oral intake. She has been catheterised long term for retention. She has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. She lives in residential aged care and is normally fully ambulant. On arrival she is rousable to voice but disoriented. Her urinalysis shows leukocytes and nitrites, and the urine in the bag is cloudy. Blood cultures have been taken. Her venous blood gas has just come back from the analyser.

The ED team is preparing the immediate resuscitation plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.6°C
data_table.Examination: Rousable to voice, disoriented; warm peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; chest clear; suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.31, lactate 4.2 mmol/L; creatinine 145 micromol/L (baseline 110); urine leukocytes and nitrites; blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hour-1 sepsis bundle intervention?

options.text: Give a 250 mL crystalloid fluid challenge and reassess before any further fluid resuscitation begins.
Defer fluid resuscitation pending CT scan to identify the source of sepsis before resuscitating.
Commence noradrenaline 0.05 mcg/kg/min as the very first intervention before any fluid bolus is given.
Give an IV stat dose of hydrocortisone 200 mg as first-line therapy for the haemodynamic instability.
Give 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid IV; commence broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour; recheck lactate at 2 hours.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman who recently arrived from Vietnam attends a refugee health clinic. She has had 3 weeks of dry cough, low-grade fevers in the evenings, drenching night sweats, and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. Her QuantiFERON-Gold Plus test is positive. The clinic registrar wants to know whether to treat as latent or active tuberculosis. The chest radiograph shows right upper lobe airspace opacity with a small cavity, and three early-morning sputum samples have been sent for acid-fast smear, culture, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR. HIV testing is negative. The first sputum smear is just back as positive for acid-fast bacilli.

She has no other significant medical history and lives in shared accommodation with one other adult.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 37.8°C
data_table.Examination: Thin; right upper zone fine crackles; no clubbing; no peripheral lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive; CXR right upper lobe airspace opacity with cavity; sputum AFB smear positive; HIV negative; LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months as latent tuberculosis treatment with monthly LFT monitoring.
Defer all treatment until liquid culture confirms drug susceptibility before any therapy commences.
Isolate, notify the public health unit, and start four-drug therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
Start rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months as a short-course latent tuberculosis regimen now.
Start moxifloxacin monotherapy 400 mg daily while awaiting susceptibility testing on the sputum specimen.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 28 hours of fever, dry cough, headache, and myalgia. Her temperature peaked at 38.8°C. She has COPD on tiotropium and salbutamol with one hospital admission in the last year for an exacerbation. She has not received the seasonal influenza vaccine this year and there are confirmed influenza A cases in her residential community. The nasal swab influenza A PCR is positive. Her oxygen saturation is 93% on room air and her chest is clear. She has had no recent overseas travel. CXR shows no consolidation.

The ED team is considering antiviral therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Mild respiratory distress; chest scattered wheeze with no crackles; no oral thrush
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A PCR positive; CXR no consolidation; FBC WCC 9.2 x10^9/L; CRP 42 mg/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold oseltamivir because the 48 hour window from symptom onset has now closed for benefit.
Start zanamivir inhaled 10 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line over oseltamivir for this patient.
Start amantadine 100 mg twice daily for 5 days targeting influenza A neuraminidase replication.
Start oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days because she is high risk despite 28 hours of symptoms.
Provide supportive care alone with paracetamol and oral fluids until symptoms resolve over coming days.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease maintained on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon, plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily, presents to the emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy. She has been unable to keep her oral hydrocortisone down. She has not taken her stress dose. She is now drowsy. Her bedside glucose is 3.2 mmol/L and a venous blood gas has just returned. The triage nurse has placed two large-bore IV cannulas and bloods are off to the lab.

The ED registrar is preparing the next interventions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen soft, mildly tender
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L; potassium 5.4 mmol/L; glucose 3.2 mmol/L; creatinine 142 micromol/L; VBG pH 7.31, lactate 2.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20 mg AM and 10 mg PM; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms mane

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Double her oral hydrocortisone dose to 40 mg and observe for 4 hours before discharging home with follow-up.
Give dexamethasone 4 mg IV stat alone and wait for cortisol level result before any IV fluid therapy.
Give 3 percent saline 100 mL to correct hyponatraemia before starting any glucocorticoid replacement therapy.
Commence fludrocortisone 200 micrograms orally now and hold IV steroids pending early morning cortisol.
Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat, commence 0.9 percent saline at 1 L over the first hour, and treat hypoglycaemia.

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 18 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia, and progressive confusion. He has hypertension and a remote left middle cerebral artery stroke with mild residual right-sided weakness. On arrival he opens his eyes to pain, says inappropriate words, and localises to pain (GCS 11). He has neck stiffness, no rash, and a new right-sided gaze preference. His pupils are 3 mm and reactive bilaterally with no papilloedema. Two large-bore IV cannulas are in. Blood cultures, FBC, U+E, coagulation, glucose, and lactate have been drawn.

The ED registrar is debating LP timing, antibiotic timing, and adjuvant steroid timing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102/min, blood pressure 168/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.1°C
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E2 V3 M5); meningism; new right gaze preference; pupils 3 mm reactive; no papilloedema; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures drawn; WCC 18 x10^9/L; CRP 220 mg/L; INR 1.0; glucose 6.4 mmol/L; lactate 2.0 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next sequence of actions?

options.text: Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV, ceftriaxone 2 g IV, and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV, then arrange urgent CT brain before LP.
Perform immediate lumbar puncture, then give dexamethasone and ceftriaxone after the CSF specimen is in hand.
Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV and obtain CT brain first; defer dexamethasone until LP confirms bacterial pathogen.
Give dexamethasone, ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and aciclovir empirically while waiting for CT and LP results.
Mannitol 1 g/kg IV plus intubation to control intracranial pressure before any antibiotic therapy is delivered.

stem: A 58-year-old man with no prosthetic valve presents with four weeks of fevers, night sweats, and fatigue. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve. Today his blood pressure is 124/68 mmHg, pulse 104, temperature 38.4°C. New early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. He has splinter haemorrhages and a small embolic stroke on MRI. Three sets of blood cultures have been collected over an hour. Transthoracic echo shows a 9 mm mobile vegetation on the aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation. He has no penicillin allergy. The microbiology service has been informed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 124/68 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97%, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur LSE, splinter haemorrhages bilaterally, no Roth spots
data_table.Investigations: Three sets of blood cultures collected; TTE: 9 mm vegetation aortic valve with mild AR; MRI brain: small acute embolic infarct

lead_in: Which empirical antimicrobial regimen is most appropriate while cultures are pending?

options.text: Vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg loading IV with gentamicin 1 mg/kg q8h as adjunct
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily monotherapy until cultures speciate the organism
Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV q4h plus flucloxacillin 2 g IV q4h plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg q8h
Daptomycin 6 mg/kg daily IV with rifampicin 600 mg orally twice daily
Wait for blood culture results before commencing any antibiotic therapy

subtopic_detail: Adjunctive corticosteroid in Pneumocystis pneumonia with hypoxaemia
stem: A 34-year-old man with a new HIV diagnosis has three weeks of exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has taken no treatment yet. Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.9, HR 104, RR 26, BP 112/70, SpO2 89 percent room air
data_table.Investigations: CD4 60 cells per microlitre; LDH 480 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: High dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with oral prednisolone
High dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole without a corticosteroid
Intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin for community pneumonia
Antiretroviral therapy started today with supportive oxygen alone
Intravenous pentamidine with oral prednisolone as first choice

subtopic_detail: Weighing preventive therapy against hepatotoxicity risk in an older adult
stem: A 74-year-old man born in Vietnam has a positive interferon gamma release assay found during screening for volunteer work. He is asymptomatic. He drinks four standard drinks daily and takes no immunosuppressive medicines.

data_table.Examination: Well, no weight loss, no cough, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive; chest radiograph normal; liver function tests normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptom education without preventive antimicrobial therapy
Isoniazid with pyridoxine for six to nine months
Rifampicin daily for four months with liver test monitoring
Annual chest radiography for the next five years
Sputum culture now and again in three months' time

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with rigors, confusion, and one day of dysuria. Pulse rate 124, blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.4°C. Mean arterial pressure is 63 mmHg. Lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. He has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid over 60 minutes. He has had blood cultures, urine cultures, and piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV within the hour. After fluid resuscitation his blood pressure is 92/56 mmHg (MAP 68 mmHg) and his repeat lactate is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 92/56 mmHg (MAP 68 mmHg) post-fluids, RR 24, SpO2 96% on 4 L NP, temperature 38.6°C
data_table.Examination: Mottled lower limbs, capillary refill 4 seconds, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L (down from 4.8), creatinine 168 micromol/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, urine culture pending
data_table.Medications: 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid given; piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence IV noradrenaline infusion via central venous access to target MAP at least 65 mmHg
Administer further 30 mL/kg crystalloid before considering any vasopressor
Add vancomycin 25 mg/kg IV empirically without an MRSA risk assessment
Give IV hydrocortisone 50 mg six hourly before any vasopressor is started
Transfuse one unit of packed red blood cells targeting haemoglobin at 100 g/L

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection LRINEC intermediate
stem: A 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of left thigh pain disproportionate to a small abrasion sustained gardening. The thigh is tense, dusky, and exquisitely tender beyond the visible erythema, with sensory loss over a 6 cm area and crepitus on palpation. Pulse rate 122, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.6°C. Bloods: WCC 16 x10^9/L, CRP 180 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 154 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, haemoglobin 132 g/L. LRINEC score totals 6.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 97%, temperature 38.6°C
data_table.Examination: Left thigh tense dusky tender beyond visible erythema, 6 cm area of sensory loss, crepitus palpable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16, CRP 180 mg/L, Na 132, creatinine 154 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, Hb 132 g/L; LRINEC 6 (intermediate)
data_table.Medications: Nil regular; IV access x2 with 500 mL Hartmann's running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: CT thigh with contrast and admit for observation if no fascial gas is seen
Urgent surgical exploration and debridement plus IV meropenem and clindamycin
Observe for 6 hours with serial LRINEC scoring before deciding on surgery
Treat as severe cellulitis with IV flucloxacillin and elevate the limb only
Commence hyperbaric oxygen therapy at the regional centre prior to debridement

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation presents with 36 hours of fever, myalgia, headache, and dry cough during a confirmed influenza A community outbreak. She has not received the seasonal influenza vaccination this year. Pulse rate 102, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.6°C. She has clear breath sounds and a normal fetal heart rate. Rapid antigen test for influenza A is positive. She has no significant comorbidities.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96%, temperature 38.6°C, FHR 140
data_table.Examination: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no chest pain, uterus appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A RAT positive; chest X-ray not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Zanamivir inhaled twice daily preferred over oseltamivir in pregnancy
Symptomatic management with paracetamol and review in 48 hours
Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days commenced today
IV peramivir as the standard parenteral option for outpatient pregnancy
Empirical amoxicillin-clavulanate added to cover bacterial co-infection

stem: A 49-year-old man is referred with a 4.5 cm right adrenal mass detected incidentally on CT for renal colic. He gives a history of episodic palpitations, sweating, and headaches over the last 18 months. His 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are: normetanephrine 8x upper limit of normal, metanephrine 5x upper limit of normal. Plasma metanephrines confirmed elevated. Endocrine surgery has been consulted for laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Current pulse 86 (peaks at 134 during episodes), blood pressure 158/96 mmHg (peaks 220/120).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86 baseline (peaks 134), BP 158/96 baseline (peaks 220/120), RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26, no orthostatic measurement yet, no other abnormality
data_table.Investigations: 24-hour urinary normetanephrine 8x ULN, metanephrine 5x ULN; plasma metanephrines confirmed elevated; CT abdomen right adrenal mass 4.5 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preoperative pharmacological preparation?

options.text: Start oral amlodipine 5 mg daily as the sole agent prior to surgery
Start oral metoprolol 50 mg twice daily and titrate to heart rate under 90
Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy without any pretreatment
Start oral phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily and titrate up over 1-2 weeks
Start IV labetalol infusion for combined alpha and beta blockade

stem: A 44-year-old woman has resistant hypertension on three agents (perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg). Her blood pressure today is 162/98 mmHg. She has a serum potassium of 3.1 mmol/L without diuretic-induced losses. She is asymptomatic. She is not pregnant. She has no family history of endocrine disease. She has been off spironolactone, beta-blocker, and direct renin inhibitor for at least four weeks. Her morning aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR) on indapamide is markedly elevated at 65 (cut-off 30 for screen positive).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 162/98 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: BMI 26, no proximal weakness, no bruit, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 142 mmol/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, ARR 65 (cut-off 30 positive); free metanephrines pending
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat ARR after 6 weeks off all antihypertensives including amlodipine
Proceed directly to CT adrenal protocol without confirmatory suppression test
Adrenal vein sampling now for lateralisation before any other confirmation
Empirical spironolactone 25 mg daily with no further investigation
Saline infusion suppression test or oral salt loading with 24-hour urinary aldosterone

stem:
A 64-year-old man presents with sudden tearing interscapular pain radiating to the chest 45 minutes ago. He has uncontrolled hypertension. Examination shows a blood pressure difference of 28 mmHg between arms. There is a faint early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He has a strong pulse in both groins. Chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy.

He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 178/108 mmHg right arm, 150/96 mmHg left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Faint early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, equal groin pulses
data_table.Investigations: CXR widened mediastinum; ECG sinus rhythm LVH; troponin pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first investigation?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT angiogram chest, abdomen, and pelvis
Transthoracic echocardiogram at the bedside immediately
Transoesophageal echocardiogram in the emergency department
MR angiogram aorta with non-contrast diffusion sequences
D-dimer for risk stratification before any imaging

stem:
A 42-year-old presents to ED with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. She is drowsy (GCS 13). There are no focal neurological signs. She has no rash. She has no immunocompromise. CT brain prior to lumbar puncture is normal. Lumbar puncture shows turbid CSF with neutrophil predominance (WCC 2200 x10^6/L, 95% neutrophils), protein 2.4 g/L (0.15-0.40), glucose 1.4 mmol/L with simultaneous serum glucose 6.0 mmol/L.

The ED registrar has IV access established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97%, temperature 39.4°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, neck stiffness, no rash, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: CSF turbid, WCC 2200 x10^6/L 95% neutrophils, protein 2.4 g/L, glucose 1.4 mmol/L (serum 6.0); CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: IV dexamethasone with first dose of ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g
IV ceftriaxone 2 g alone without any corticosteroid adjunct
IV vancomycin monotherapy while awaiting susceptibility result
IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg without any antibacterial cover concurrently
Delay all antibiotics until CSF Gram stain result is available

stem:
A 32-year-old presents with one episode of haematemesis 12 hours ago after binge drinking and forceful vomiting. He has had no further bleeding. He has no melaena. He has no comorbidities and takes no regular medications. Bloods: haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), urea 5.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 76 micromol/L (60-110), INR 1.0 (0.9-1.2). Examination is unremarkable. His Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0.

He wishes to go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no tenderness, no signs of chronic liver disease, no melaena on PR
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L, urea 5.4 mmol/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with safety netting plus outpatient gastroscopy
Admit and perform urgent inpatient gastroscopy within 4 hours
Admit overnight for observation with serial haemoglobin checks
Start IV pantoprazole 80 mg bolus then infusion 8 mg/hour as inpatient
Transfuse 1 unit packed red cells empirically before discharge

stem:
A 38-year-old woman presents with one week of fatigue, bruising, and intermittent confusion. She has no recent infection. Bloods: haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165), platelets 18 x10^9/L (150-400), reticulocytes 6.2% (0.5-2.5), LDH 1820 U/L (140-280), unconjugated bilirubin 42 micromol/L (3-21), creatinine 138 micromol/L (45-90). Coombs test negative. Blood film shows 8 schistocytes per high power field. ADAMTS13 activity is sent. INR is 1.0.

The haematology team has been called urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.4°C
data_table.Examination: Pallor, petechiae, intermittent confusion, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 18 x10^9/L, retics 6.2%, LDH 1820 U/L, bilirubin 42 micromol/L (unconjugated), creatinine 138 micromol/L; Coombs negative; film 8 schistocytes/hpf; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plasma exchange and pulse methylprednisolone, awaiting ADAMTS13 result
Platelet transfusion to platelets >100 x10^9/L before any other intervention
Cyclophosphamide induction prior to any plasma exchange therapy
Eculizumab as first-line for presumed atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Observation pending ADAMTS13 result before further therapy

stem:
A 48-year-old man with known Addison disease has had gastroenteritis for two days. He vomited his morning hydrocortisone. He now presents drowsy with abdominal pain. Bloods: sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110). He has hyperpigmentation. He is on usual maintenance hydrocortisone 20-10-10 mg daily and fludrocortisone 100 mcg.

IV access has been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucous membranes, hyperpigmented buccal mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124, potassium 5.7, glucose 3.1, urea 12.4, creatinine 142
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20-10-10 mg daily, fludrocortisone 100 mcg (missed today)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 30 min
IV dexamethasone 8 mg only with maintenance crystalloid fluid
Restart oral hydrocortisone 30 mg and observe in ED short stay
IV insulin and dextrose infusion to correct hyperkalaemia first
Hypertonic 3% sodium chloride 100 mL over 30 minutes for hyponatraemia

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with three weeks of haemoptysis, fatigue, sinusitis, and progressive dyspnoea. Creatinine has risen from 78 to 312 micromol/L (60-110) over two weeks. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein with red cell casts. Chest CT shows bilateral nodular and cavitating lesions. PR3-ANCA is strongly positive at 142 U/mL (normal less than 5). MPO-ANCA is negative. He has no fever, no recent infection, no haemodynamic instability, and no overt pulmonary haemorrhage. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis.

He has consented to immunosuppression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 95%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Saddle nose deformity, sinus tenderness, bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 312 micromol/L (rose from 78), urinalysis 3+ blood 2+ protein red cell casts, PR3-ANCA 142 U/mL, MPO-ANCA negative, CT bilateral nodular cavitating lesions, renal biopsy pauci-immune crescentic GN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction regimen?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone pulse for 3 days then rituximab weekly induction
Methotrexate 25 mg weekly with prednisolone 30 mg daily induction
Plasma exchange alone without any concurrent immunosuppression
Mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily as monotherapy induction
Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily with prednisolone 60 mg daily

stem:
A 68-year-old presents with two weeks of bone pain, fatigue, and progressive confusion. Bloods: haemoglobin 84 g/L (130-180), creatinine 384 micromol/L (60-110), calcium 3.4 mmol/L corrected (2.10-2.55), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), total protein 96 g/L (60-80). Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG kappa M-band of 42 g/L. Serum free light chain ratio kappa/lambda 220 (normal 0.26-1.65). Skeletal survey shows lytic lesions in the skull and pelvis. He is hypovolaemic with mild AKI on dipstick proteinuria 2+.

Haematology and renal teams have been consulted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 97%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Pallor, dry mucous membranes, confused (MMSE 22/30)
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 84 g/L, creatinine 384 micromol/L, calcium 3.4 mmol/L corrected, total protein 96 g/L, IgG kappa M-band 42 g/L, kappa/lambda ratio 220, skeletal survey lytic lesions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management priority?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 3 L over 4 hours plus bortezomib regimen
IV zoledronic acid 4 mg as the immediate priority for hypercalcaemia
Pamidronate 90 mg IV without prior fluid resuscitation hydration
Plasma exchange as monotherapy for free light chain removal
Urgent haemodialysis with high cut-off filter without chemotherapy

stem:
A 62-year-old man presents to ED at 02:00 with 4 hours of central chest tightness radiating to the left jaw. He has hypertension and hyperlipidaemia and smokes 15 cigarettes daily. The pain partially settled with sublingual GTN but has now returned.

The baseline 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with minor T-wave flattening laterally but no ST elevation. The initial high-sensitivity troponin T at 0 hours is 18 ng/L (URL 14 ng/L). A repeat at 1 hour is 32 ng/L. Renal function is normal and there is no recent significant illness or chronic kidney disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic during pain, dual heart sounds with no murmur, chest clear, no calf swelling
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm with lateral T-wave flattening, 0-hour hs-cTnT 18 ng/L (<14), 1-hour hs-cTnT 32 ng/L (delta 14 ng/L), eGFR 88 mL/min, electrolytes within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, sublingual GTN PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous thrombolysis with tenecteplase as he meets ACS criteria with raised troponin
Rule out NSTEMI on these troponin values and discharge home with GP follow-up
Plan repeat troponin at 6 hours and admit only if the 6-hour value remains elevated
Arrange outpatient computed tomography coronary angiography within the next week
Diagnose NSTEMI, give DAPT plus parenteral anticoagulant, and refer for early invasive angiography

stem:
A 35-year-old presents to an outer-suburban GP clinic 15 minutes after eating cashew nuts at a restaurant. He has known peanut allergy and now reports tightness in his throat and difficulty breathing. He has urticarial wheals over his trunk and arms. He is alert but anxious.

He has no diagnosed cardiac disease. He has no regular medications. His weight at his last GP visit was 80 kg. The practice has a single 1 mg/mL adrenaline ampoule and a 1 mL syringe; an EpiPen and EpiPen Jr are also stocked.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 28 with audible wheeze, SpO2 92% in air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, perioral swelling, expiratory wheeze bilaterally, no stridor, alert, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside only, ECG sinus tachycardia, no other immediate results

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 1:1000 0.3 mg IM (300 mcg) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeatable
Adrenaline 1:1000 0.5 mg IM (500 mcg) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeatable
Adrenaline 1:10 000 1 mg IV (1000 mcg) bolus over 1 minute by intravenous access
Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV plus chlorphenamine 10 mg IV before any adrenaline dose
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with face mask oxygen and admit to the local hospital ward

stem:
A 24-year-old presents to ED 6 hours after taking what she states was 30 paracetamol 500 mg tablets in a single ingestion. She is now nauseated but not vomiting. There is no co-ingestion identified on history or urine drug screen, and she takes no regular medications. She weighs 60 kg.

A paracetamol level taken on arrival at 6 hours post-ingestion is 200 mg/L. INR is 1.1. ALT and creatinine are within normal limits. The treating nomogram in your ED is the Australian Rumack-Matthew '150 line' (paracetamol 150 mg/L at 4 hours).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly nauseated, no abdominal tenderness, no jaundice, no encephalopathy, alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol 200 mg/L at 6 hours, INR 1.1 (0.8-1.2), ALT 28 U/L (5-30), creatinine 70 micromol/L (60-110), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold N-acetylcysteine because the level is below the standard 200 mg/L 4-hour line
Commence intravenous N-acetylcysteine using the 21-hour two-bag Australian protocol
Administer single-dose activated charcoal 50 g orally before any NAC is started
Repeat the paracetamol level at 12 hours and start NAC only if the level is still high
Refer immediately for haemodialysis to remove circulating paracetamol from the blood

subtopic_detail: Threshold for stopping isoniazid when transaminases rise during preventive therapy
stem: A 41-year-old woman is six weeks into isoniazid with pyridoxine for latent tuberculosis. She feels well, with no nausea, abdominal pain or jaundice, and takes no other medicines. Her scheduled liver function tests are reported below.

data_table.Examination: Well, no jaundice, no right upper quadrant tenderness
data_table.Investigations: ALT 340 U/L (baseline 28), ALP 110 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease isoniazid now and repeat the liver tests
Continue isoniazid and repeat the liver tests weekly
Halve the isoniazid dose and repeat the liver tests
Continue isoniazid and add ursodeoxycholic acid daily
Switch to rifampicin today and repeat tests in a month

stem:
A 42-year-old with Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg evening, plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily, presents 18 hours into a gastroenteritis illness. She has had 8 episodes of vomiting and has not been able to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose. She did not have her steroid emergency injection at home because the family could not find it.

On arrival to the emergency department she is drowsy but rousable. She is afebrile. Her abdomen is soft. There is no chest or respiratory infection identified clinically.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 82/48 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, no peritonism, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.4), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), VBG pH 7.30 HCO3 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 0.9% saline bolus 1 L over 30 minutes
Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg now and reassess in 2 hours after rehydration with oral fluids
Intravenous fludrocortisone 100 mcg with isotonic saline 500 mL over the first hour
Intravenous insulin and dextrose to correct hyperkalaemia before any steroid is given
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% over 10 minutes before fluid resuscitation

stem:
A 42-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria, and Kussmaul breathing after running out of insulin 36 hours ago. He weighs 80 kg. He has had no recent diuretic use and no chronic gastrointestinal losses other than the current vomiting.

Venous blood gas shows pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L. Capillary glucose is 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L. Sodium is 138 mmol/L. Critically, the initial potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and the ECG shows ST depression with a U wave. He is alert and orientated (GCS 15) and has IV access in place. The standard ADS DKA pathway is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 32 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, alert, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritonism
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected anion gap 24, ECG ST depression with U waves
data_table.Medications: Insulin glargine (ran out), insulin aspart (ran out)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV saline 1 L plus 40 mmol potassium chloride over 1 hour; hold insulin until K ≥3.5 mmol/L
IV insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h commencing immediately at recognition of DKA
IV sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol bolus to correct severe acidosis before insulin or fluids
IV 0.9% saline 2 L bolus then immediate insulin infusion before any potassium replacement
Subcutaneous insulin aspart 10 units stat plus oral potassium replacement in 200 mL water

stem:
A 48-year-old presents to your endocrinology outpatient clinic for review. She was diagnosed with a unilateral 4 cm right adrenal mass on a CT abdomen done after recurrent panic-like episodes. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated, consistent with phaeochromocytoma. Her GP started metoprolol 50 mg twice daily one week ago to control her tachycardia.

Her home BP readings have actually worsened, ranging 165-180 systolic and 100-110 diastolic. She has no history of asthma. She is awaiting surgical planning. She has no other medications and no significant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 172/108 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No bruits, no thyromegaly, no acanthosis, no orthostatic drop measured today, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free normetanephrine 4500 pmol/L (<900), CT abdomen 4 cm right adrenal mass, UEC and FBC within normal limits, ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Medications: Metoprolol 50 mg twice daily (started 1 week ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Plan immediate surgical adrenalectomy this week without further antihypertensive change
Continue metoprolol and add phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, escalating as tolerated
Increase metoprolol to 100 mg twice daily and add amlodipine 5 mg daily for BP control
Stop metoprolol now and start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, titrated to symptoms
Substitute hydralazine 25 mg three times daily for metoprolol and continue current plan

stem:
A 64-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan ED at 0900 with central chest tightness that started at 0700 and has now resolved. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a 30 pack-year smoking history. Her father had an MI at 55. Initial ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no ST changes or T-wave inversion.

Her first hs-troponin is back, and a second draw at one hour is now available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, no respiratory distress, chest clear, normal heart sounds with no murmurs, no peripheral oedema, calves soft
data_table.Investigations: ECG: normal sinus rhythm, no ST changes; hs-troponin T at 0 hours 8 ng/L (sex-specific 99th percentile 14 ng/L), 1-hour hs-troponin T 9 ng/L; renal function within normal limits; chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nocte; no aspirin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for serial troponin testing every 6 hours for 24 hours
Commence dual antiplatelet therapy and admit to coronary care
Discharge home for outpatient cardiology with cardiac stress test
Activate the cath lab for urgent coronary angiography now
Order a CT coronary angiogram before discharge planning

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia SMART-COP and ICU admission
stem:
A 68-year-old man with COPD on tiotropium presents with a 3-day history of productive cough, fever, and rigors. He is admitted from ED to a general medical ward. Six hours later he becomes more dyspnoeic and the registrar is called.

He has not had any antibiotics in the last 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 88% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Confused (AMTS 4/10), accessory muscle use, right-sided crackles, no wheeze, well-perfused but cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: dense right lower lobe consolidation with small parapneumonic effusion. ABG on 6 L/min: pH 7.32, pO2 56 mmHg, pCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 19 mmol/L; lactate 4.2; WCC 22 x10^9/L; albumin 26 g/L; sodium 132 mmol/L; urea 10.2 mmol/L; creatinine 102 micromol/L; CRP 318 mg/L
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium 18 micrograms daily; ED ceftriaxone 2 g + azithromycin 500 mg PO given on arrival 6 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bridge to non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP and reassess in 2 hours
Continue ceftriaxone monotherapy on the ward with 2 hourly review
Insert intercostal drain for the small parapneumonic effusion
Calculate SMART-COP and refer to ICU for likely intubation and inotropic support
Discharge with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate after 24-hour observation

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with no provoking risk factors presents with mild right-sided chest discomfort. CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) reports a single subsegmental pulmonary embolus in the right lower lobe with no proximal involvement. Bilateral leg ultrasound is negative for DVT. She has no haemodynamic compromise, no right heart strain on echocardiogram, and a normal troponin. She has no cancer, no recent surgery, no immobility, and no oestrogen exposure.

The respiratory and vascular teams have reviewed the imaging and discussed treatment options with her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, no respiratory distress, chest clear, calves soft and non-tender, no chest wall tenderness
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: solitary subsegmental PE in right lower lobe, no main pulmonary artery / lobar / segmental PE; lower limb Doppler bilateral negative; D-dimer raised; troponin within normal limits; echocardiogram normal RV function; FBC unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg daily indefinitely
Commence warfarin with INR target 2 to 3 for at least 6 months
Withhold anticoagulation with surveillance lower limb Doppler weekly for 2 weeks
Commence apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD for 3 months total
Treat with LMWH for 5 days then warfarin for 3 months at INR 2 to 3

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic selection for cystitis when the potassium is already at risk
stem: A 72-year-old woman has two days of dysuria and frequency. She has stage 3 chronic kidney disease and takes perindopril and spironolactone for heart failure. She has no loin pain, no vomiting and no rigors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80 /min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick nitrite and leucocyte positive; potassium 5.2 mmol/L last week; eGFR 52 mL/min

lead_in: Which oral antibiotic is most appropriate?

options.text: Nitrofurantoin orally for five days
Trimethoprim orally for three days
Amoxicillin with clavulanate for five days
Ciprofloxacin orally for three days
Doxycycline orally for seven days

stem:
A 38-year-old man with known epilepsy on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily is brought to ED having had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure that has been ongoing for 25 minutes. Paramedics gave intramuscular midazolam 10 mg en route (10 minutes ago), with no cessation of seizure. He has not had a seizure in 6 months and his last lamotrigine level was therapeutic.

Intravenous access has been obtained on arrival, and he is being managed in the resuscitation bay with continuous monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130, BP 152/96 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Generalised tonic-clonic activity ongoing, foaming at mouth, no head trauma, pupils midpoint and reactive, no focal lateralising signs
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.22 lactate 5.8 glucose 6.4 mmol/L; UEC and FBC pending; lamotrigine level pending
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 200 mg BD; IM midazolam 10 mg given 10 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg over 10 minutes
Wait 15 minutes to observe for spontaneous seizure cessation
Commence intravenous fosphenytoin 20 mg/kg phenytoin equivalents
Repeat intravenous midazolam 10 mg and reassess after 5 minutes
Proceed straight to rapid sequence intubation with thiopentone infusion

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection imaging choice with renal impairment
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset tearing inter-scapular chest pain radiating to the back. He has a history of hypertension on irbesartan 300 mg daily, polycystic kidney disease with baseline eGFR 28, and bicuspid aortic valve. He is haemodynamically stable but anxious. He has a 3 cm aneurysm of the ascending aorta on a previous echocardiogram 12 months ago.

The ED registrar has reviewed him and the on-call cardiothoracic surgical team has been contacted. Imaging is being planned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 188/108 mmHg right arm / 142/86 mmHg left arm, RR 22, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Distressed with pain, blood pressure differential right arm vs left arm 46 mmHg systolic, diastolic murmur at right upper sternal border, no neurology, calves soft, equal pulses bilaterally on radial and femoral
data_table.Investigations: Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows intimal flap visible in ascending aorta and mild aortic regurgitation; creatinine 220 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 188); chest X-ray widened mediastinum; troponin within normal limits; ECG normal sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next imaging step?

options.text: Proceed to MRI angiography of the thoracic and abdominal aorta urgently
Commence intravenous labetalol infusion and admit to cardiology ward for observation
Proceed directly to operating theatre on the basis of the bedside TTE findings
Insert intraaortic balloon pump as a bridge to definitive surgery now
Proceed to CT angiography of the thoracic and abdominal aorta with iodinated contrast

subtopic_detail: Refractory hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state - insulin and fluid choice
stem:
An 84-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide is brought in by his family after 5 days of decreased oral intake from a viral illness. He is now drowsy and oriented only to person. The ED registrar has resuscitated him with 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride over 2 hours, and a maintenance insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour was started 90 minutes ago. His glucose has fallen from 48 to 44 mmol/L. He still has minimal urine output (10 mL/hr).

His paired osmolality is being recalculated and the intensive care team is reviewing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 96/64 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 4 L/min, temperature 37.4 °C, weight 72 kg
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, no peritonism, no focal neurology, no diabetic foot infection
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 44 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), Na 152 mmol/L (135-145), corrected Na 162 mmol/L, K 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarb 22 mmol/L, anion gap 12, ketones 0.4 mmol/L (<0.6), urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (60-110), measured osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (275-295), lactate 2.6
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1g BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily; 2L 0.9% saline given; insulin infusion 0.05 unit/kg/hour running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Double the insulin infusion to 0.1 unit/kg/hour to accelerate glucose decline
Stop the insulin infusion and continue saline-only until glucose below 30 mmol/L
Switch to 5% dextrose / 0.9% sodium chloride and continue insulin infusion at current rate
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol over 30 minutes for acidosis
Switch to 0.45% sodium chloride and continue insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hour

stem:
A 71-year-old man is reviewed in general practice. He had an incidental finding of a 4.2 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm on CT 18 months ago during workup of suspected renal calculi. He has had two surveillance ultrasounds, the most recent today. He has hypertension on perindopril, dyslipidaemia on atorvastatin, type 2 diabetes well-controlled on metformin (HbA1c 6.8%), and a 45 pack-year smoking history; he quit 3 years ago. He has no abdominal pain, no back pain and no syncope.

Today's surveillance ultrasound shows an infrarenal AAA measuring 5.4 cm in maximal anteroposterior diameter, an increase of 0.7 cm from 12 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, pulsatile mass palpable in upper abdomen, no peritonism, femoral and pedal pulses palpable, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; lipid profile total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, LDL 2.4 mmol/L; HbA1c 6.8% (7.4-8.4 individualised target met); recent CT angiogram from 18 months pending re-imaging
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nocte, metformin 1000 mg BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance with general practitioner follow-up review
Add aspirin 100 mg daily and re-image in 12 months as routine vascular surveillance
Arrange immediate emergency department presentation for haemodynamic monitoring now
Refer to vascular surgery for assessment of elective endovascular or open aneurysm repair
Add a beta-blocker to reduce aneurysm growth and review again in 12 months' time

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 28 weeks gestation is reviewed in the emergency department with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness that began an hour ago while shopping. She has no prior VTE and no thrombophilia. Her two previous pregnancies were uncomplicated. She does not smoke. Her chest X-ray is clear and there is no pneumothorax. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Her lower-limb compression ultrasound is normal.

She remains haemodynamically stable but tachycardic. The obstetric medicine and respiratory registrars are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate 145 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: Mildly distressed, no calf swelling, no asymmetric leg pain, clear chest, no JVP elevation, no parasternal heave, gravid uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, no S1Q3T3 or RV strain; chest X-ray clear bilateral lung fields; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; troponin negative; arterial blood gas pH 7.46, PaO2 78 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, on room air; lower limb compression ultrasound negative bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat lower-limb compression ultrasound in 7 days and treat empirically if positive
Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan as first-line lung imaging modality in pregnancy
CT pulmonary angiogram as the first-line definitive imaging modality in pregnancy
Pulmonary angiogram in interventional radiology as the next imaging modality used
Empirical therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban orally without confirmatory imaging

subtopic_detail: Adjunctive therapy when hyperkalaemia accompanies a severe metabolic acidosis
stem: A 60-year-old man with oliguric acute kidney injury has had intravenous calcium followed by insulin with dextrose for hyperkalaemia. The renal team is preparing him for dialysis, which is at least two hours away.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.9 mmol/L; pH 7.12; bicarbonate 9 mmol/L; creatinine 420 micromol/L

lead_in: Which additional treatment is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate alongside the current therapy
High dose intravenous furosemide alongside the current therapy
Nebulised salbutamol repeated every twenty minutes
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate every six hours
A second dose of intravenous calcium gluconate now

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with a 3-month history of episodic headaches, palpitations and diaphoresis presents to the emergency department with severe headache and chest pain. Her GP referred her two weeks ago to endocrinology for ?phaeochromocytoma after recording a BP of 198/112 mmHg in clinic; 24-hour fractionated plasma metanephrines were markedly elevated (normetanephrine 8.2 nmol/L; reference <0.71). A CT abdomen showed a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass. Her appointment is scheduled in 9 days. She has not yet been started on alpha-blockade.

Her usual medications include ramipril and metoprolol prescribed for the hypertension by her GP. The medical registrar is at the bedside in the resuscitation cubicle.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 232/126 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min via nasal prongs, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, anxious, severe pounding headache, no focal neurology, pupils equal and reactive, no papilloedema, cardiac auscultation S1 S2 with a soft systolic flow murmur, no peripheral oedema, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia with no ST changes; troponin pending; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; CT brain shows no acute haemorrhage; urinalysis no proteinuria
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 10 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily (started 4 weeks ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase metoprolol to 100 mg twice daily and add hydralazine 25 mg orally as an add-on
Commence intravenous phentolamine 2 to 5 mg bolus with doses titrated to blood pressure
Administer intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus titrated to blood pressure as first agent
Administer intravenous amlodipine infusion at 5 mg per hour as a calcium channel blocker
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus then 1 g per hour as primary agent

stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic venous insufficiency presents to the emergency department with a 36-hour history of rapidly spreading right leg pain and redness. He had a small dog bite on the shin 4 days ago that he managed at home with washing and a bandaid. Now the pain seems out of proportion to what he can see. He has rigors and feels very unwell. He has had no recent travel and no IV drug use.

On arrival the triage nurse fast-tracks him to the resuscitation cubicle. The surgical and medical registrars are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Right leg shin to mid-thigh deep dusky erythema with poorly demarcated margins, severe tenderness extending well beyond the area of erythema, areas of grey-blue discolouration with bullae forming, foul-smelling exudate, no crepitus, no femoral or popliteal lymphadenopathy distally
data_table.Investigations: WCC 24 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP 320 mg/L (<5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 92), sodium 130 mmol/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, lactate 4.2; CK 1820 U/L (<200); LRINEC score calculated as 9 (high-risk); plain X-ray right leg no gas in tissues; lactate venous 4.2
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1000 mg BD, atorvastatin 40 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Resuscitate, IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin, urgent surgery
Admit, mark erythema borders, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly, review in 6 hours
Arrange urgent CT with contrast of the right lower limb before any surgical referral
Give intramuscular benzylpenicillin 1.2 g for presumed streptococcal cellulitis only
Give a single dose of oral clindamycin 600 mg with admission for observation overnight

stem:
A 54-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR positive, on pyridostigmine 60 mg every 4 hours and prednisolone 20 mg daily) is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Over the last 3 days she has had a productive cough and has been increasing her pyridostigmine dose without medical advice because her weakness has been worse. Today she became more dyspnoeic, diaphoretic and developed abdominal cramps with diarrhoea. Her partner reports increased oral secretions.

On arrival she is fatigued but alert. The neurology and ICU registrars are at the bedside; she has been moved to the resuscitation cubicle and a bedside FVC is being measured.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 92% on 8 L/min via face mask, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, increased oral secretions and lacrimation, miosis with sluggish reaction, generalised muscle weakness MRC 3/5 in all limbs, neck flexion weakness, fasciculations present in upper limbs, abdominal cramps, no rash, no fever above 37.6, no ptosis change documented, FVC 0.85 L (predicted 3.2 L), negative inspiratory force -18 cmH2O (target more negative than -30)
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.30, pCO2 56, PaO2 68 mmHg on FiO2 0.5, HCO3 26; CK 320 U/L (<200); chest X-ray small right basal infiltrate; ECG sinus bradycardia with no AV block
data_table.Medications: Pyridostigmine increased from 60 mg every 4 hours to 90 mg every 3 hours by patient over the last 24 hours; prednisolone 20 mg daily, mycophenolate 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine dose to 120 mg every 3 hours and start intravenous plasma exchange
Administer intravenous neostigmine 0.5 mg as a confirmatory edrophonium-equivalent test
Withhold pyridostigmine, give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and prepare for intubation
Withhold pyridostigmine, atropine 0.5 to 1 mg IV for muscarinic features, prepare to intubate
Administer pralidoxime 30 mg/kg intravenously as a cholinesterase reactivator agent

stem:
A 38-year-old woman is admitted to the high-dependency unit with progressive ascending weakness over the last 5 days. She had gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago with documented Campylobacter on stool culture from her GP. Her weakness began as foot tingling, then ankle weakness, climbing proximally. She now cannot stand without assistance. She has not had any cranial nerve involvement until this morning, when she developed mild bilateral facial weakness. She has noticed labile blood pressure and has had two brief episodes of marked tachycardia followed by transient bradycardia today.

Bedside FVC 1.4 L (predicted 3.0 L) and is trending down. The neurology and ICU registrars are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse fluctuates between 50 and 130 over the last hour, BP fluctuates between 168/96 and 92/56 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Lower limb power MRC 2/5 distally and 3/5 proximally, upper limb power 4/5 throughout, bilateral mild facial weakness, areflexia in all four limbs, glove-and-stocking sensory loss to vibration and proprioception, FVC 1.4 L (down from 2.0 L 8 hours ago), no cough impairment yet, no swallowing difficulty
data_table.Investigations: Lumbar puncture protein 1.8 g/L (<0.45) with cell count 4/microL (albuminocytologic dissociation); MRI lumbar spine shows enhancement of cauda equina nerve roots; nerve conduction studies pending; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; ECG bradycardia at present without AV block

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin (HbA1c 6.8% last month), no prior MRSA, and no penicillin allergy. He is systemically well, afebrile, and has a clear margin on the cellulitis that you outline with a marker.

On examination there is a 12 cm by 8 cm area of warmth, erythema, and tenderness on the medial right shin without lymphangitic streaking, abscess, or crepitus. Distal pulses are intact and sensation is preserved. There is no necrosis, bullae, or pain disproportionate to examination.

A 68-year-old woman attends your GP clinic for review after a minimal-trauma distal radius fracture sustained 6 weeks ago. She is otherwise well, post-menopausal since age 51, with no fragility fractures previously. Her mother had a hip fracture at age 72. She is on no regular medications. Her renal function is normal (eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73 m^2), serum calcium 2.36 mmol/L, vitamin D 78 nmol/L, and PTH within normal limits.

DEXA scan shows lumbar spine T-score -2.7 and femoral neck T-score -2.5. FRAX 10-year hip fracture probability is 6.2% and major osteoporotic fracture 14.5%. She has good dental health with no upcoming invasive dental procedures. She prefers oral therapy.

A 28-year-old woman presents to your neurology clinic 3 weeks after acute onset of blurred vision and pain on movement of her right eye lasting 10 days, now resolving. There is no preceding viral illness, no recent travel, and no family history of demyelinating disease. She has a 6-month-old breastfed child and is otherwise well.

On examination today her visual acuity is 6/9 right and 6/6 left with a relative afferent pupillary defect on the right. Fundoscopy shows mild right optic disc pallor. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. MRI brain demonstrates three periventricular and one juxtacortical T2 hyperintense lesion with no enhancement on gadolinium; MRI cervical spine shows one short-segment lesion. CSF reveals oligoclonal bands positive in CSF, absent in serum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/9, left 6/6, right RAPD positive, mild right disc pallor, no internuclear ophthalmoplegia, no nystagmus, motor and sensory examination normal, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: 3 periventricular + 1 juxtacortical T2 lesions, no gadolinium enhancement; MRI cervical spine: 1 short-segment T2 lesion; CSF: oligoclonal bands positive in CSF (negative in serum), normal cell count, glucose, protein; aquaporin-4 IgG and MOG-IgG negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency myelopathy with subacute combined degeneration
Clinically isolated syndrome alone, not yet meeting MS criteria
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) as the proposed approach
MOG antibody disease with the proposed clinical action
Multiple sclerosis (relapsing-remitting) by 2017 McDonald criteria

A 52-year-old woman with established AChR antibody-positive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 60 mg six times daily and prednisolone 20 mg daily is brought to the emergency department with worsening dyspnoea, dysphagia, and bilateral ptosis. She had a mild upper respiratory infection 5 days ago, and her treating neurologist increased her pyridostigmine from 4 to 6 doses daily 2 days ago.

In the emergency department she is anxious and breathless with shallow respirations. She has bilateral ptosis, weak shoulder abduction, and difficulty swallowing her saliva. Her pupils are 3 mm and reactive, mucous membranes are dry, and bowel sounds are normal. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.32, pCO2 56 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg on room air, with bedside FVC measured at 1.0 L (predicted 3.4 L).

A 62-year-old man with long-standing hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history presents to the emergency department with sudden severe interscapular and chest pain that began 90 minutes ago while gardening. He describes it as tearing in quality, peaking immediately at onset. He has no nausea, no diaphoresis, and no exertional component. He has no known prior cardiovascular event.

In the resuscitation bay, his right arm BP is 168/96 mmHg and left arm BP is 132/82 mmHg. Pulse 88, regular. Chest auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge. ECG shows sinus rhythm with non-specific lateral T-wave flattening. Bedside troponin is below the rule-in threshold. Chest X-ray shows widening of the upper mediastinum. He is hypertensive, alert, and orientated.

data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, no carotid bruit, peripheral pulses intact bilaterally, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus, non-specific lateral T flattening; troponin <5 ng/L; chest X-ray widened mediastinum; D-dimer pending; FBC and creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for urgent coronary angiogram for suspected NSTEMI as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action

Bolus IV glyceryl trinitrate without rate control to lower blood pressure rapidly as the proposed approach

A 28-year-old tall thin man is brought into the emergency department after sudden onset right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath 30 minutes ago while playing basketball. He has no past history. On arrival he is alert but pale and diaphoretic. His trachea is shifted to the left, the right hemithorax is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and his jugular venous pressure is markedly elevated.

He rapidly deteriorates with hypotension and worsening hypoxia. Pulse 138, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather. A bedside lung ultrasound shows absent lung sliding and a 'barcode sign' on the right.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Trachea deviated to left, right hemithorax hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, JVP elevated, peripheral cool, no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: Bedside lung ultrasound: absent lung sliding right, barcode sign right; ECG sinus tachycardia; chest X-ray deferred for time-critical management

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Pericardiocentesis under ultrasound guidance as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
Urgent chest X-ray before any intervention as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as the proposed clinical action
Endotracheal intubation and positive-pressure ventilation to improve oxygenation as the proposed approach

Needle decompression of the right hemithorax in the 4th-5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line, followed by intercostal catheter

A 58-year-old woman is referred to your respiratory clinic with progressive right-sided pleural effusion. She had a thoracic spine T8-T10 fusion 6 weeks ago for traumatic vertebral compression after a motor vehicle accident. She has lost 4 kg since surgery and is mildly breathless on exertion. Diagnostic pleural aspiration today yields 60 mL of milky white fluid.

Fluid biochemistry returns later: pleural total protein 38 g/L (serum 65 g/L), pleural LDH 280 U/L (serum 220 U/L, upper normal 250), pleural pH 7.42, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, cell count 1900 cells/microL with 92% lymphocytes. Pleural cholesterol 1.8 mmol/L. Cytology shows mature lymphocytes with no malignant cells.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Stony dull right base with reduced breath sounds and decreased tactile fremitus, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema, no palpable lymphadenopathy, thoracic spine surgical scar healing
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid: milky white, total protein 38 g/L (serum 65 g/L), LDH 280 U/L (serum 220), pH 7.42, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, cell count 1900 cells/microL with 92% lymphocytes; cholesterol 1.8 mmol/L; cytology mature lymphocytes; CT thorax pending

options.text: Pleural fluid amylase; raised amylase confirms pancreatic pleural fistula
Pleural fluid cholesterol confirms chylothorax if above 5.18 mmol/L

Pleural fluid Gram stain and culture; positive culture confirms empyema
Send pleural fluid triglyceride; a level above 1.24 mmol/L confirms chylothorax

He has had no recent travel, no aspiration risk, no immunosuppression, and no prior pneumonia.

On examination he is alert. The chest has right basal crackles with bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion. There is no asterixis. A 67-year-old man attends your general practice clinic with 4 months of progressive fatigue and dyspnoea on exertion. He says 'I get puffed bringing in the shopping now, when last winter I was still walking the dog up the hill'. He has not noticed any rectal bleeding, melaena, change in bowel habit, abdominal pain, or weight loss. He has no past gastrointestinal disease. He is a non-smoker, drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, and his diet is balanced.

On examination he is pale with no signs of heart failure. Per-rectal examination reveals no mass and faecal occult blood is positive on point-of-care testing. FBC shows haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180), MCV 72 fL (80-100), MCH 24 pg (27-32). Ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 7% (16-45%). LFTs and UEC are within normal limits. He is haemodynamically stable. His grandparents were Mediterranean but he has never been investigated for haemoglobinopathy; his haemoglobin 3 years ago was 142 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no signs of heart failure, abdomen soft non-tender, no organomegaly, per-rectal no mass, faecal occult blood positive
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180), MCV 72 fL (80-100), MCH 24 pg (27-32), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 7% (16-45%); LFTs and UEC within normal limits

options.text: Empirical oral iron supplementation for 12 weeks and arrange repeat FBC and ferritin assessment then
Test for haemoglobin electrophoresis and HbA2 for beta-thalassaemia trait given his Mediterranean family history
Refer for upper endoscopy and colonoscopy under one anaesthetic session for source of blood loss
Order CT colonography with intravenous contrast as the only screening investigation needed at this stage
Send urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori and treat empirically with eradication if positive on testing

subtopic_detail: New atrial fibrillation rate control and anticoagulation
stem:
A 73-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic with 3 days of palpitations and exertional breathlessness. She says 'my heart has been racing on and off, and the chemist found my pulse was all over the shop'. She has a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine, type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and previous transient ischaemic attack 5 years ago that was managed conservatively. She has no chest pain, no syncope, and no symptoms suggesting heart failure.

On examination her pulse is irregularly irregular at 124 bpm. Heart sounds are dual with no murmurs. Chest is clear. There is no peripheral oedema. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 124 bpm, no ischaemic ST changes, and QRS 90 ms. TSH 2.0 mIU/L; electrolytes, renal and liver function within normal limits; haemoglobin 132 g/L. Bedside echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function with no significant valvular disease. CHA2DS2-VA score is calculated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 irregularly irregular, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no murmur, no signs of heart failure, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation HR 124 bpm, no ST changes; TSH 2.0 mIU/L; UEC and LFTs within normal limits; haemoglobin 132 g/L; bedside echo preserved LV function, no significant valvular disease
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Electrical cardioversion this admission and discharge home on aspirin alone for the long-term stroke prophylaxis
Commence intravenous heparin infusion and refer for transoesophageal-guided cardioversion within 24 hours
Refer urgently for pulmonary vein isolation ablation procedure and commence aspirin pending the catheter laboratory date
Add bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily for rhythm control and arrange repeat ECG and routine review in 6 weeks without other therapy
Commence apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily for rate control, and refer cardiology for outpatient rhythm decision

stem:
A 54-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department resuscitation bay by ambulance with sudden-onset dyspnoea and pre-syncope. Her partner says 'she just stood up after the long flight home this morning and went pale and dizzy'. She had a knee arthroplasty 3 weeks ago. She has no history of bleeding, no stroke, no recent surgery within 2 weeks, and no malignancy. She is currently taking enoxaparin prophylactic dose at home.

On examination she is dyspnoeic. There is no leg swelling. JVP is raised at 7 cm. Cardiac auscultation reveals a loud P2 and right ventricular heave. Chest is clear. Bedside echocardiogram shows right ventricular dilatation with septal flattening and a McConnell sign of preserved apical contractility with akinetic basal-mid right ventricular free wall. ECG shows sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern, and right axis deviation. A point-of-care CT pulmonary angiogram, completed within 10 minutes of arrival, confirms saddle pulmonary embolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 84/56 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on room air rising to 94% on 10 L oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Dyspnoeic, JVP 7 cm, loud P2, right ventricular heave, no leg swelling, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside echo: RV dilatation, septal flattening, McConnell sign; ECG sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3, right axis deviation; CTPA saddle PE; troponin 0.4 microgram/L (under 0.04); haemoglobin 128 g/L; platelets 220 x10^9/L; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours as systemic thrombolysis for haemodynamically unstable PE
Commence intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion at therapeutic rate and admit to the high-dependency unit
Refer for inferior vena cava filter placement before any antithrombotic therapy is administered to this patient
Increase enoxaparin to 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily and admit for haemodynamic monitoring overnight
Trial fluid resuscitation alone with 2 L normal saline and reassess haemodynamic and respiratory status in 60 minutes

stem:
A 47-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by her partner after 3 days of vomiting, abdominal pain, and increasing weakness. He says 'she's been getting darker on her hands and her gums all winter, but she didn't want to bother the doctor'. She has no past psychiatric history. She has been losing weight, feeling weak, and has had postural symptoms. She has no diarrhoea, no fever, and no recent travel.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. She has hyperpigmentation in her palmar creases and gums, with skin tanning over light-exposed areas. There is no goitre. Her abdomen is soft, mildly tender, and there are no signs of peritonism. Bloods show sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 6.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), and pH 7.30 on a venous blood gas with bicarbonate 19 mmol/L. She has had no morning cortisol or ACTH check before. Septic screen is sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 84/52 mmHg supine and 70/40 mmHg standing, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, hyperpigmentation palmar creases and buccal mucosa, postural drop, soft mildly tender abdomen, no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (135-145), K 6.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), VBG pH 7.30, HCO3 19 mmol/L; FBC, septic screen, paired random cortisol and ACTH samples sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wait for the morning cortisol level to return before any glucocorticoid is administered to confirm diagnosis first
Commence intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg as the immediate steroid choice, followed by intravenous saline resuscitation
Administer intravenous 50% dextrose 50 mL for the hypoglycaemia and review the haemodynamics after that single bolus
Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat with intravenous normal saline resuscitation and glucose correction
Refer urgently for adrenalectomy after CT imaging today and arrange intensive care admission before any pharmacological treatment

stem:
A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to your emergency department with 24 hours of nausea, vomiting, and breathlessness. She says 'my insulin pump alarmed yesterday afternoon, and I thought I'd just put a new line in this morning, but I haven't been able to eat'. She has no chest pain, no infection symptoms, and no recent surgery. She is alert and oriented.

On examination she has Kussmaul breathing and dry mucous membranes. There is no focal neurological deficit. Bloods show glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L (under 0.6), pH 7.18, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected sodium 138 mmol/L, anion gap 24, creatinine 105 micromol/L, urea 8 mmol/L. data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 28 with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first intervention?

options.text: Intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour as a single first intervention prior to fluid resuscitation
Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour while preparing insulin infusion and potassium replacement
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.3 unit/kg bolus immediately and arrange admission to the high-dependency unit

Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily as antibiotic cover given the prevalence of infection as a DKA trigger

stem:
A 78-year-old man presents to your emergency department with sudden right-sided weakness and headache that started 60 minutes ago. He has atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and a mechanical mitral valve replacement 5 years ago. He says 'the room started spinning, then I couldn't lift the right arm at all'. His regular medications are warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5 for the mitral mechanical valve), bisoprolol, and ramipril. His most recent INR 1 week ago was 2.8.

On examination GCS is 14 (E4 V4 M6). Right-sided hemiparesis power 1/5 upper and 2/5 lower, with right facial droop and dysarthria. Non-contrast CT head shows a 25 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage with no midline shift and no intraventricular extension. INR returns at 7.0. Platelet count 180 x10^9/L. There is no clinical evidence of mechanical valve thrombosis, no fever, and no recent infection. He has had no falls or trauma. He has had no procedures or surgery recently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 178/96 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), right hemiparesis power 1/5 arm and 2/5 leg, right facial droop, dysarthria, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT head 25 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage, no midline shift, no intraventricular extension; INR 7.0; platelets 180 x10^9/L; haemoglobin 138 g/L; UEC normal; troponin negative
