data_table.Medications: Warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5), bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate haemostatic intervention?

options.text: Administer fresh frozen plasma 4 units intravenously as the only haemostatic intervention for the elevated INR today
Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg as the only intervention given the high INR and the clear ICH on imaging today
Withhold warfarin alone and recheck the INR in 6 hours before administering any further haemostatic interventions then
Administer recombinant activated factor VII 90 micrograms/kg intravenously as the immediate haemostatic intervention
Administer intravenous prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg as the immediate combined reversal

stem:
A 68-year-old man is brought to your emergency department by ambulance with 6 hours of confusion and rigors. His wife says 'he was shivering, then he went pale and floppy on the couch and stopped making sense'. He has a background of type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 140 micromol/L). He has not had recent surgery. He has had increasing urinary frequency and dysuria over the past 3 days.

On examination he is drowsy and disoriented to time and place, with mottled peripheries, a capillary refill of 4 seconds, and warm core. There is no neck stiffness. Abdomen is soft with left renal angle tenderness. Bedside lactate is 4.6 mmol/L (under 2.0). VBG shows pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), HCO3 18 mmol/L (22-26). FBC shows WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 16.2 (2.0-7.5), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-450). Creatinine 220 micromol/L (45-90), CRP 240 mg/L (under 5). Urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte 3+. He has received 250 mL of normal saline en route.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 regular, BP 84/52 mmHg (MAP 63 mmHg), RR 28, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, disoriented x2, mottled peripheries, CRT 4 seconds, left renal angle tenderness, no rash, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L (under 2.0); VBG pH 7.30 bicarbonate 18 mmol/L; WCC 18.4 with neutrophilia, platelets 96 x10^9/L; creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 140); CRP 240 mg/L; urine nitrites positive leukocyte 3+
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; gliclazide MR 60 mg daily; perindopril 4 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Send blood cultures, give IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose plus IV ampicillin, and 1 L crystalloid fluid bolus
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as first-line therapy for the septic shock physiology immediately
Take blood cultures, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid over the first 3 hours, IV piperacillin-tazobactam, lactate trend, and call ICU
Hold antibiotics until urine culture returns a positive organism and titrate fluid by hourly central venous pressure
Commence noradrenaline immediately before any fluid resuscitation to restore mean arterial pressure to 65 mmHg

stem:
A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your emergency department with 36 hours of severe left thigh pain and erythema, having scraped his shin on a metal gate at work 2 days ago. He says 'the pain is way worse than the redness looks, paracetamol does nothing, and now my whole leg feels numb in patches'. He has had a fever overnight and one episode of vomiting this morning. His diabetes is managed with metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor.

On examination he is pale and unwell. The left thigh is erythematous, swollen, exquisitely tender, with patchy dusky areas and a single haemorrhagic blister on the antero-medial surface. Crepitus is palpable along the medial thigh. Sensation is reduced over the medial aspect of the thigh. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. WCC 21 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 280 mg/L (under 5), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 156 micromol/L (45-90), glucose 16.4 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L. LRINEC score is 9.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 regular, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Erythematous swollen left thigh with patchy duskiness, haemorrhagic blister antero-medially, palpable crepitus medially, reduced sensation over medial thigh
data_table.Investigations: WCC 21 x10^9/L, CRP 280 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 156 micromol/L, glucose 16.4 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, Hb 122 g/L; LRINEC 9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; dapagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Computed tomography of the thigh with intravenous contrast to delineate the extent of fascial gas before referral
Intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin and admit under general medicine for serial limb examinations
Urgent surgical referral for theatre debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics including clindamycin, and fluid resuscitation
Outline the erythema and discharge home on oral cefalexin with review by general practitioner in 24 hours
Apply topical mupirocin and adjacent silver sulfadiazine dressings with daily wound clinic review for 1 week

stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman attends your general practice clinic with a recent low-trauma right wrist fracture sustained from a slip in her garden. She says 'I fell on my outstretched hand from standing height onto grass'. She has a background of well-controlled hypertension and a long history of cigarette smoking (now ceased 8 years). She had her menopause at age 51 and has not been on hormone therapy.

On examination she is well, with healed wrist plaster removed last week. She is 162 cm tall (down 4 cm from her self-reported peak height of 166 cm). She has no kyphosis on visual inspection. There is no thoracic spine tenderness. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry done after the fracture shows lumbar spine T-score -2.6 and femoral neck T-score -2.8. Bloods show 25-hydroxyvitamin D 58 nmol/L (over 50 sufficient), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), phosphate 1.0 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR 70 mL/min/1.73 m squared. Thyroid function and parathyroid hormone are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Healed right wrist fracture, height 162 cm (peak 166), no spine tenderness, no visible kyphosis
data_table.Investigations: DEXA: lumbar T-score -2.6, femoral neck T-score -2.8; 25-OH vitamin D 58 nmol/L (>50); corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); phosphate normal; PTH and thyroid function normal; eGFR 70 mL/min/1.73 m^2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone for 12 months and repeat DEXA before any further treatment
Commence raloxifene 60 mg orally daily as the first-line pharmacological therapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis
Commence denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous every 6 months as the first-line therapy with twice-daily calcium-rich diet
Refer to endocrinology for teriparatide as first-line anabolic therapy in this older postmenopausal woman
Commence oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly with calcium and vitamin D and address modifiable risk factors

stem:
You are the medical registrar in the resuscitation bay. A 24-year-old motorcyclist has been brought in after a high-speed collision with a parked vehicle. The paramedics report 'he was found unconscious at the scene, with a deformed pelvis and obvious open right tibial fracture, and is bleeding heavily from the leg'. A pelvic binder has been applied and tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously was given on the way.

On arrival he is now responsive only to painful stimuli (GCS 8). His airway is patent with a Yankauer to manage blood. He is tachypnoeic and shocked. There has been an obvious large external blood loss from the right thigh and a tense haematoma over the pelvis with pelvic tenderness. The chest is clear with bilateral air entry; FAST shows no free fluid in the abdomen and no pericardial effusion. Right tibial bone is visible at the wound. He has had 1.5 L of warmed crystalloid and his blood pressure remains 78/40 mmHg. Bedside haemoglobin 92 g/L from arterial sampling; venous lactate 5.4 mmol/L (under 2.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 regular, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 30, SpO2 96% on 15 L/min via non-rebreather, temperature 35.4 °C, GCS 8
data_table.Examination: Tense pelvic haematoma, open right tibial fracture, ongoing bleeding from leg wound, no abdominal free fluid on FAST, no pneumothorax
data_table.Investigations: Bedside Hb 92 g/L, lactate 5.4 mmol/L; coags pending; trauma series imaging being arranged
data_table.Medications: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV in pre-hospital; warmed crystalloid 1.5 L now in

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue warmed crystalloid resuscitation to a systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg before considering blood products
Transfuse 4 units of packed red cells alone and reassess before requesting any plasma or platelets
Activate the massive transfusion protocol, transfuse a 1:1:1 ratio of red cells, FFP and platelets, and call for trauma team review
Hold transfusion until a formal coagulation screen and fibrinogen result returns to guide product selection
Administer prothrombinex 50 IU/kg as primary haemostatic resuscitation in major haemorrhage before any blood

stem:
A 38-year-old man is brought to your emergency department with 12 hours of severe headache, fever, neck stiffness, and photophobia. His partner says 'he didn't go to work, then this evening he became drowsy and confused'. He has no immunosuppressive condition, no recent overseas travel, and no head injury. He had received the meningococcal ACWY and B vaccines in adolescence.

On examination he is drowsy (GCS 13), febrile, with marked neck stiffness, Kernig sign positive on the right, and Brudzinski sign positive. There is no focal neurological deficit, no papilloedema, no cranial nerve abnormality, and no rash. Fundoscopy is clear. Bedside lactate 2.6 mmol/L (under 2.0); fingerprick glucose 4.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures are taken now and an immediate CT head (because of the altered conscious state) is being arranged with the radiologist; lumbar puncture will follow if no contraindication. He has had no antibiotics yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116 regular, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 °C, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, neck stiffness, Kernig positive right, Brudzinski positive, no rash, no focal deficit, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L; blood cultures taken; CT head being arranged; LP planned post-CT

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait for the CT head and lumbar puncture results to return before commencing any antimicrobial or steroid therapy
Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g now and defer dexamethasone until pneumococcal infection is confirmed
Commence intravenous vancomycin alone empirically for ceftriaxone-resistant pneumococcal coverage immediately
Administer IV dexamethasone 10 mg followed immediately by IV ceftriaxone 2 g (plus IV benzylpenicillin if listeria risk)
Refer to neurology for outpatient lumbar puncture and viral PCR before any antibiotic decision today

stem:
A 72-year-old man is brought to your emergency department by ambulance 90 minutes after sudden onset right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia. His wife says 'he was trying to ask for tea and the words came out scrambled, his right arm went limp and his face drooped'. The last known well time is documented at 90 minutes ago. He has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.8%), hypertension on perindopril 8 mg, and atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily; the last apixaban dose was at 6 am yesterday (32 hours ago). He has not had recent surgery or bleeding events.

On examination he has dense right-sided weakness (NIHSS 14), right facial droop, expressive aphasia, and right homonymous hemianopia. There is no neck stiffness and no other focal neurological deficit. A non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage and a hyperdense left MCA sign without established infarct; CT angiography demonstrates a left M1 MCA occlusion. Bloods show platelets 222 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, creatinine 88 micromol/L, glucose 8.4 mmol/L, anti-Xa level low (consistent with last apixaban dose 32 hours ago). His current blood pressure is 198/108 mmHg confirmed on two readings 10 minutes apart.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 irregularly irregular, BP 198/108 mmHg confirmed on two readings, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: NIHSS 14, dense right hemiparesis, right facial droop, expressive aphasia, right homonymous hemianopia
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT head no haemorrhage with hyperdense left MCA sign; CTA left M1 MCA occlusion; platelets 222, INR 1.0, glucose 8.4 mmol/L, anti-Xa low
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily; apixaban 5 mg BD (last dose 32 hours ago); metformin 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to intravenous alteplase at current blood pressure without any antihypertensive intervention now
Administer intravenous labetalol 10 mg or IV glyceryl trinitrate aiming for blood pressure under 180/105 mmHg, then proceed with thrombolysis
Withhold alteplase entirely due to recent apixaban exposure within the prior 48 hours regardless of anti-Xa level result
Reduce blood pressure with intravenous labetalol 10 mg to a target under 185/110 mmHg, give alteplase, and refer for thrombectomy
Commence intravenous heparin infusion at full anticoagulation dose for atrial fibrillation-related ischaemic stroke

stem:
A 52-year-old man is referred to your endocrinology clinic after investigation for resistant hypertension with paroxysms of headache, palpitations, and sweating. He says 'my blood pressure shoots up out of nowhere, my heart pounds, and I drench my shirt'. Twenty-four hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are 4 times the upper limit and plasma metanephrines are confirmatory. Computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast shows a 4.5 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass with high attenuation on the non-contrast images and avid contrast enhancement. He has no family history but genetic testing is pending. Today he attends for management planning. He is otherwise well, with no chest pain, no postural symptoms, and no ECG abnormalities at rest.

On examination his BP at rest is 168/104 mmHg and rises to 192/118 mmHg when he stands suddenly. Pulse is 88. There is no cardiac murmur and no carotid bruit. Fundoscopy shows grade 2 hypertensive changes. Bloods show normal electrolytes, normal creatinine, glucose 5.6 mmol/L, normal calcium. He is currently on amlodipine 10 mg daily only. He asks about preparation for the planned right adrenalectomy in 2 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 regular, BP 168/104 mmHg supine and 192/118 mmHg on rapid stand, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy, no cardiac murmur, no postural drop, no acute neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines elevated; 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines 4 x ULN; CT adrenal 4.5 cm right mass with high non-contrast attenuation and avid enhancement; genetic testing pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Commence atenolol 50 mg orally daily as preoperative blockade for the planned right adrenalectomy procedure
Continue amlodipine 10 mg as monotherapy for blood pressure control and proceed with right adrenalectomy in two weeks as planned
Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg orally twice daily, titrate to symptom and BP control, then add beta blocker for tachycardia
Phenoxybenzamine titrated to mild postural drop and nasal stuffiness, salt and fluid liberalisation, then a beta blocker after alpha blockade
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion preoperatively as the sole pharmacological preparation needed

stem:
A 68-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced 11 months ago is admitted to your medical ward with 3 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats, and 4 kg weight loss. His wife says 'he's been getting these sweats that drench through his pyjamas at night'. He has had no recent dental procedure but uses a removable upper denture. He has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.4%) on metformin.

On examination he has temperature 38.4 °C and a new aortic regurgitation murmur (decrescendo early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge). He has a single Osler node on the right index finger pulp and conjunctival petechiae. There is no peripheral oedema. The lung bases are clear. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn 30 minutes apart from separate venipunctures; one set has already grown gram-positive cocci in clusters within 14 hours. Transthoracic echocardiogram (image quality limited by body habitus) shows a possible 8 mm mobile mass on the aortic bioprosthesis. Transoesophageal echocardiogram is booked for tomorrow morning. Renal function is creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110); the patient has no known beta-lactam allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 122/58 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: New aortic regurgitation diastolic murmur, single Osler node right index finger, conjunctival petechiae, no peripheral oedema, clear lung bases
data_table.Investigations: Three sets of blood cultures drawn; 1 of 3 grown gram-positive cocci in clusters at 14 hours; TTE shows possible 8 mm mobile mass on aortic bioprosthesis; creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110); HbA1c 7.4%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g once daily for 6 weeks targeting streptococci with periodic infection markers
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly monotherapy targeting methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus only
Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin, plus rifampicin empirically pending blood culture identification and sensitivities
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg 8-hourly for community-acquired endocarditis cover
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly with empiric metronidazole pending culture identification

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection medical management
stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to your emergency department with sudden severe interscapular pain. He says 'it felt like someone stabbed me in the back and now it's tearing down to my hip'. His past medical history includes hypertension on amlodipine and bicuspid aortic valve (no surgery). He smokes 20 cigarettes per day.

On examination he is alert but diaphoretic. Blood pressure is 188/108 mmHg in both arms, equal. Pulses are present and symmetric in all four limbs with no asymmetry. There is no focal neurological deficit. Chest auscultation is clear and the abdomen is soft. CT angiogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows an intimal flap originating distal to the left subclavian artery extending to the iliac bifurcation, with no aortic root or arch involvement. There is no end-organ malperfusion (renal arteries patent, mesenteric vessels patent, spinal cord signs absent). There is no contrast extravasation and no pericardial effusion. His ECG is normal sinus rhythm without ischaemic changes. He has not had previous aortic surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 188/108 mmHg equal in both arms, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert diaphoretic, equal limb pulses, no focal neuro deficit, clear chest, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: CT angiogram intimal flap distal to left subclavian extending to iliac bifurcation, no end-organ malperfusion, no contrast extravasation, no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate sodium nitroprusside infusion alone targeting mean arterial pressure under 70 mmHg
Activate cardiothoracic surgery emergent for open repair of distal aortic dissection within 60 minutes
Discharge with outpatient cardiology follow-up and oral perindopril titration once pain has settled at home
Commence intravenous labetalol titrated to heart rate under 80 bpm and systolic 130-140 mmHg as targets
Commence intravenous labetalol or esmolol titrated to heart rate under 60 bpm and systolic blood pressure 100-120 mmHg

stem:
A 24-year-old man, 188 cm tall and thin (BMI 19), presents to your emergency department with 6 hours of sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. He says 'it just started when I was watching TV, and breathing in makes it worse'. He has no past medical history, no trauma, and is not a smoker. He is in his first job in IT and lives at home with his parents.

On examination he is alert and in moderate distress. Tracheal position is central. Right hemithorax has reduced air entry and hyper-resonant percussion in the upper zone. There is no surgical emphysema. He is haemodynamically stable. CT chest shows a primary right-sided pneumothorax with a 3.5 cm gap between the lung edge and the chest wall at the level of the hilum, no parenchymal disease, and no haemothorax. There is no contralateral abnormality. He has not been on any flights and has no diving or aviation occupation. He is not planning to fly within the next 2 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, moderate distress, trachea central, right reduced air entry with hyper-resonant percussion, no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: CT chest: right primary pneumothorax 3.5 cm gap at the hilum, no parenchymal disease, no haemothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial high-flow oxygen alone with serial chest X-rays at 6-hour intervals and discharge if reabsorbing
Insert an 8-14 French intercostal catheter with underwater seal and observe in a respiratory short-stay ward
Insert a 28 French chest drain with underwater seal and add suction at minus 20 cmH2O immediately
Refer for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery pleurodesis as the first-line management of large primary pneumothorax
Aspirate with a 16 G cannula in the second intercostal space midclavicular line and observe in the department

stem:
A 47-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with 10 weeks of bilateral hand and wrist pain. She says 'my fingers are so stiff in the morning that I can't open the kettle for almost 2 hours, and it's getting worse'. She has had no skin rashes, no oral ulcers, and no Raynaud's phenomenon. She has no family history of inflammatory arthritis. She works as a school librarian and finds typing increasingly painful.

On examination she has symmetrical swelling and tenderness of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally, both wrists, and both metacarpophalangeal joints with positive squeeze test. There is no synovitis at the distal interphalangeal joints or in the spine. The 28-joint disease activity score (DAS28) is 5.2 (high). Investigations show ESR 48 mm/h (under 20), CRP 32 mg/L (under 5), rheumatoid factor 198 IU/mL (under 14), anti-CCP antibody 156 U/mL (under 7), ANA negative, hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, latent TB screen QuantiFERON negative. Plain X-rays of the hands show periarticular osteopenia with no erosions yet. Hand ultrasound shows synovial hypertrophy and power Doppler signal in the affected joints.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical PIP, wrist, and MCP synovitis bilaterally, positive squeeze test, no DIP involvement, no spine involvement
data_table.Investigations: DAS28 = 5.2 high, ESR 48 mm/h (under 20), CRP 32 mg/L (under 5), RF 198 IU/mL (under 14), anti-CCP 156 U/mL (under 7), HBsAg negative, HCV negative, QFT-Plus negative, X-rays: periarticular osteopenia no erosions, US: synovial hypertrophy with power Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and review the response over the next 8 weeks before further escalation
Refer to rheumatology and start oral prednisolone 50 mg daily as monotherapy pending the specialist consultation
Refer urgently to rheumatology; commence methotrexate 10-15 mg daily with folic acid, bridge prednisolone, and review at 12 weeks
Refer urgently to rheumatology; commence methotrexate 10-15 mg weekly with folic acid, bridge prednisolone, and review at 12 weeks
Commence hydroxychloroquine monotherapy as first-line DMARD and reserve methotrexate for refractory disease only

stem:
A 36-year-old man is admitted to your medical unit with 2 days of fever, sore throat, painful red eyes, and a spreading rash. His partner says 'his lips have gone all crusty and he can't open his eyes properly because of the discharge'. He started lamotrigine 25 mg daily 3 weeks ago for bipolar II disorder and his sertraline was continued from 6 months prior. He took the lamotrigine dose escalation at the standard 2-weekly intervals per the AMH schedule. He has had no other new drugs.

On examination he has 14% body surface area dusky erythematous targetoid lesions on the trunk and proximal limbs with central pallor. Nikolsky sign is positive (gentle lateral pressure shears the upper epidermis). He has crusted lips, oral mucosal erosions, conjunctival injection with purulent discharge, and erosions of the glans penis. There is no scalp involvement. He is alert but distressed. His weight is 72 kg and the Wallace rule of nines estimates 14% body surface involvement (less than 30% threshold for TEN).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: 14% BSA dusky targetoid lesions with central pallor, positive Nikolsky sign, crusted lips and oral erosions, purulent conjunctivitis, glans erosions, no scalp involvement
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 86 micromol/L (60-110), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-26), urea 5.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), ALT 28 U/L (under 35), CRP 96 mg/L (under 5)
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 25 mg daily (started 3 weeks ago); sertraline 50 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lamotrigine at current dose, commence oral prednisolone 50 mg daily, and discharge after antihistamines
Stop lamotrigine immediately, transfer to a burns or specialist dermatology unit, and provide supportive care
Stop sertraline immediately and continue lamotrigine as the more likely culprit drug for serotonin-mediated rash
Continue lamotrigine, stop sertraline, and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as the principal therapy
Stop both drugs, commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for infected oral and conjunctival erosions, and discharge

subtopic_detail: Potassium based salt substitute as the cause of a rising potassium
stem: A 69-year-old man with stage 3 chronic kidney disease takes perindopril and feels well. Since a heart failure admission he has been cutting his sodium intake and uses a supermarket salt substitute on every meal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70 /min, blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.0 mmol/L (was 4.6); creatinine 140 micromol/L, unchanged; ECG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the salt substitute and recheck the potassium
Halve the perindopril dose and recheck the potassium
Start oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate and recheck later
Refer him urgently to the emergency department today
Continue current treatment and recheck in three months

stem:
A 56-year-old woman with known acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis is admitted to your high-dependency unit with worsening shortness of breath and difficulty swallowing over 24 hours. Her husband says 'she's been getting weaker through the day and her eyes are drooping again like the first time she was sick'. She takes pyridostigmine 60 mg every 4 hours and prednisolone 10 mg daily; she increased her pyridostigmine to every 3 hours on her own 2 days ago after feeling weaker.

On examination she is alert, with ptosis, dysarthria, and bilateral facial weakness. She has bulbar weakness with poor cough. Her pupils are 5 mm and minimally reactive, with mild watery lacrimation and increased oral secretions. Reflexes are present. Vital capacity at the bedside (by spirometry) is 0.9 L (predicted 3.5 L, severe restriction). Single-breath count is 8 (under 20 indicates significant respiratory weakness). Cardiac monitor shows sinus rhythm at 56 bpm. Her temperature is normal. She has had no recent infection. She has had no new drugs apart from her own increased pyridostigmine dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 93% on 4 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, ptosis bilaterally, dysarthria, facial weakness, poor cough, pupils 5 mm minimally reactive, lacrimation increased, oral secretions increased, present reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Bedside vital capacity 0.9 L (predicted 3.5 L), single-breath count 8 (under 20 abnormal), ABG pH 7.34 pCO2 50 mmHg pO2 78 mmHg HCO3 26 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Pyridostigmine 60 mg every 3 hours (self-increased 2 days ago from every 4 hours), prednisolone 10 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue pyridostigmine at increased dose, give intravenous methylprednisolone, and observe in the high-dependency unit
Hold pyridostigmine temporarily, intubate for airway protection if NIV fails, and commence IVIG or plasma exchange
Administer intravenous edrophonium (Tensilon) test 2 mg IV with atropine on hand to discriminate the crisis type
Trial of subcutaneous atropine 0.6 mg as the diagnostic and therapeutic step for suspected cholinergic crisis
Increase prednisolone to 60 mg orally and continue pyridostigmine at self-titrated dose with bedside review

stem:
A 67-year-old woman is admitted to your medical ward 4 hours after a witnessed cardiac arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved at 28 minutes (PEA arrest). She was the manager of a small business and her brother says 'she'd been getting more breathless over the last few weeks but kept working through it'. She was found to have a large central pulmonary embolus and received thrombolysis with alteplase.

She is now intubated and ventilated on tidal volume 6 mL/kg ideal body weight (440 mL), set rate 16, FiO2 0.5, PEEP 10 cmH2O. Her temperature is 35.6 °C. Bloods show creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110), urea 16 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), normal sodium and chloride 142 and 100 mmol/L. Her ABG shows pH 7.10, pCO2 60 mmHg (35-45), pO2 78 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L (22-26), base excess minus 10, lactate 8.2 mmol/L (under 2.0). Her anion gap (sodium minus chloride minus bicarbonate) is 24 mmol/L (8-12).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 102/64 mmHg on norepinephrine 0.08 microgram/kg/min, RR set 16 (spontaneous 22), SpO2 95% on FiO2 0.5 PEEP 10, temperature 35.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Intubated and ventilated, sedated, no spontaneous movement to noxious stimulus yet, peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: ABG pH 7.10, pCO2 60 mmHg (35-45), pO2 78 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L (22-26), base excess minus 10, lactate 8.2 mmol/L (under 2.0); sodium 142 mmol/L chloride 100 mmol/L; anion gap 24 mmol/L (8-12); creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); urea 16 mmol/L (2.5-7.5)
data_table.Medications: Norepinephrine 0.08 microgram/kg/min, propofol sedation, alteplase thrombolysis 90 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most accurate acid-base interpretation?

options.text: Pure high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation matching Winter's formula
Pure respiratory acidosis with renal compensation in the chronic phase with elevated bicarbonate response
Pure metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation and a high anion gap from volume contraction
Mixed high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (raised lactate) plus respiratory acidosis with inadequate ventilation
Triple disorder with metabolic acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, and respiratory alkalosis from haemodynamic instability

stem:
You are the registrar at a refugee health clinic seeing a 31-year-old asymptomatic man who arrived from a high TB prevalence country eight months ago. He has had a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay as part of his refugee health screening. He denies cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss or haemoptysis. He has no past history of TB and no known contact with active TB. He shares a household with his wife and two children, all of whom are well.

On examination he is well, with normal observations. Chest examination is clear and he has no lymphadenopathy. Chest radiograph today is reported as showing no parenchymal infiltrate, no upper-zone scarring, no cavitation, no hilar lymphadenopathy and no pleural effusion. HIV serology is negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits and his ALT is 28 U/L (<40). His eGFR is above 60 mL/min. He is not pregnant, is a non-drinker and is medically well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Well; clear chest; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus positive; chest radiograph clear; HIV, hepatitis B and C negative; ALT 28 U/L; FBC and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for nine months total
Rifampicin 600 mg orally daily for four months as latent TB infection treatment course
Standard active TB therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for six months
Repeat QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus in six months and only treat if conversion confirmed
No treatment given asymptomatic status with clear chest film and routine review in twelve months

stem:
You are the ED registrar seeing a 24-year-old man brought in by his housemate with a one-day history of headache, neck stiffness, fever and photophobia. He has had two episodes of vomiting. He has no past medical history, no recent travel and no immunosuppression. He had a Bexsero vaccine in his teens. The housemate also says he was confused on the drive in.

On examination he has a temperature of 38.9 °C and a Glasgow coma score of 14. He has marked neck stiffness with positive Brudzinski's sign. There is no focal neurology, no papilloedema, no rash and pupils are equal and reactive. There is no recent head injury and no immunocompromise. His airway is patent. CT head is being arranged given his confusion. Blood cultures have been taken. The intern asks if she should give antibiotics now or wait for the LP.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), confused; neck stiffness with Brudzinski positive; pupils equal reactive; no focal deficit; no rash; no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures taken; FBC, UEC pending; CT head being arranged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer IV dexamethasone 10 mg only and wait for CT to determine antibiotic choice
Defer empirical antibiotics until both CT head and lumbar puncture have been completed and CSF returned
Give IV dexamethasone 10 mg with IV ceftriaxone 2 g now, then proceed to CT head and lumbar puncture
Administer IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg only and await CSF herpes simplex virus PCR before further escalation
Administer single dose oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg for meningococcal post exposure prophylaxis only

stem:
You are the medical registrar called to assess a 72-year-old woman on the urology ward 24 hours after an elective transurethral resection of bladder tumour. The nurse has just escalated because her observations have changed over the last hour. She has a history of type 2 diabetes on metformin and hypertension on perindopril. She has no known allergies.

On arrival she is rousable to voice, drowsy but orientated, and reports rigors. Pulse is 128/min, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.9 °C. Capillary refill is 4 seconds and her extremities are cool. She has indwelling catheter drainage of cloudy urine. Bilateral chest is clear. Her abdomen is soft, mildly tender suprapubically without peritonism. Bedside venous blood gas shows lactate 4.8 mmol/L, pH 7.30, base excess -5. Urine culture from this morning has just been called as growing gram negative rods.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but orientated; CRT 4 sec, cool peripheries; clear chest; mild suprapubic tenderness; IDC draining cloudy urine
data_table.Investigations: VBG: lactate 4.8 mmol/L (<2), pH 7.30, BE -5; urine MCS gram negative rods on Gram stain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management bundle?

options.text: Hour-1 bundle: blood cultures, IV ceftriaxone plus gentamicin, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, ICU for vasopressors
Administer IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g and arrange CT abdomen before fluids or cultures are taken
Give 250 mL balanced crystalloid bolus and reassess at 30 minutes before considering further fluid
Start IV adrenaline 0.05 mcg/kg/min via peripheral line before any crystalloid fluid resuscitation today
Withhold empiric antibiotics until full microbiology sensitivities return and focus on fluid resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection BP control
stem:
You are the medical registrar called urgently to ED for a 58-year-old man with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back that started 90 minutes ago. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and is a current smoker. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 112/min with no acute ischaemic changes. Troponin is within normal limits. CT aortogram has just been completed and reports an uncomplicated type B aortic dissection arising distal to the left subclavian artery with no end-organ malperfusion, no rupture and no aortic diameter above 5.5 cm. He is talking in full sentences.

On arrival his BP is 192/104 mmHg in the right arm and 188/100 mmHg in the left arm. He has equal radial pulses. His chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender, and lower limb pulses are present and symmetric. He has had paracetamol 1 g and fentanyl 50 mcg with mild improvement in pain. The interventional radiologist and the cardiothoracic surgeon are in handover and they ask you to commence BP control. He has no asthma, no heart failure and no known allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, BP 192/104 mmHg right arm, 188/100 mmHg left arm, RR 22/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Equal radial pulses; clear chest; soft non-tender abdomen; symmetric lower limb pulses
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia 112/min no ischaemic changes; troponin within normal limits; CT aortogram: uncomplicated type B dissection distal to left subclavian, no malperfusion, no rupture, max diameter <5.5 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line BP/HR target and agent?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg bolus to reduce afterload via brisk diuresis and improve perfusion
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion targeting systolic BP 100-120 mmHg without rate control
Oral perindopril 5 mg with planned reassessment of blood pressure and heart rate in 30 minutes
Intravenous labetalol infusion titrated to systolic BP 100-120 mmHg and heart rate <60/min
Urgent endovascular stent graft regardless of complication status or current haemodynamic stability

stem:
You are the surgical registrar called to the ED for a 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide who has presented with 36 hours of progressive right lower limb redness, swelling and pain. He recalls a minor superficial scratch from gardening four days ago. He has had a fever of 38.5 °C at home and felt increasingly unwell over the last 12 hours.

On examination he is unwell, with a pulse of 116/min, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C. Erythema extends from the ankle to the mid-calf with poorly defined borders. The skin is tense and there is severe pain on light palpation that he reports as out of proportion to the visible signs. There are no obvious skin blisters, no crepitus and no necrotic patches. Bloods this morning: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 280 mg/L (<5), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 14.8 mmol/L, haemoglobin 138 g/L. He has no warfarin and no immunosuppression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Right lower limb erythema ankle to mid-calf with poorly defined borders; tense skin; pain out of proportion to visible signs; no blisters, crepitus or necrosis
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L; CRP 280 mg/L; sodium 131 mmol/L; creatinine 142 micromol/L; glucose 14.8 mmol/L; Hb 138 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order an urgent MRI of the right lower limb before any antibiotic escalation or surgical referral decision
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly and reassess clinical progress and inflammatory markers in 24 hours
Outline the erythema in marker pen, elevate the limb and repeat inflammatory blood markers in 12 hours
Urgent surgical exploration with on-call team plus IV piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin and vancomycin
Discharge home on oral cefalexin 500 mg six hourly with general practitioner review in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Sexual transmission advice when the viral load has stayed undetectable
stem: A 36-year-old man has taken a single tablet antiretroviral regimen for three years, with an undetectable viral load at every six monthly check. His female partner is HIV negative. They want to conceive and ask whether they need condoms or any medication.

data_table.Results: CD4 620 cells per microlitre; renal and liver function normal
data_table.Partner: HIV negative on testing last month; no other sexual partners

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: He will not transmit HIV sexually while the viral load stays undetectable
Condoms are still necessary because the transmission risk is reduced but not removed
She should take daily pre-exposure prophylaxis until she conceives
Sperm washing with assisted reproduction is needed for conception
He should add a fourth antiretroviral agent while they are trying

stem:
You are the inpatient medical registrar reviewing a 54-year-old woman admitted 72 hours ago with community-acquired pneumonia. She presented with five days of cough, fever and pleuritic chest pain. She was assessed in ED as SMART-COP score 3 (BP 102/68, RR 28, SpO2 91% room air, multilobar infiltrate), commenced on IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and admitted to the ward.

On day 3 of treatment she is no better. Her temperature has continued spiking to 38.8 °C twice daily. Her oxygen requirement has risen from 2 to 4 L/min nasal prongs. She has a new mild confusion that her family confirms is out of character. She has developed loose stools twice in the last 12 hours but no abdominal pain. Sodium has fallen from 138 to 128 mmol/L, ALT is now 220 U/L (was 32 U/L) and CRP has risen from 184 to 256 mg/L. Repeat chest radiograph shows progression of the right lower zone consolidation with a small new left mid zone infiltrate. Sputum cultures are negative. She returned a week ago from a hot springs holiday in the Northern Territory. Urinary Legionella antigen has not yet been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 91% on 4 L nasal prongs, temperature 38.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild confusion (new); right lower zone crackles plus new left mid zone crackles; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (was 138, ref 135-145); ALT 220 U/L (was 32, ref <40); CRP 256 mg/L (was 184); chest radiograph: progression right lower + new left mid zone; sputum culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bronchoscopy with BAL today to obtain definitive microbiological diagnosis before changing antibiotics
Escalate to IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin for nosocomial pneumonia
Continue current therapy and add IV hydrocortisone 50 mg 6-hourly for severe CAP
Send urinary Legionella antigen and switch to IV azithromycin 500 mg daily plus continue beta-lactam cover
Transfer to ICU for non-invasive ventilation without changing antibiotic regimen

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and a body mass index of 32 kg/m2 presents to your general practice with sudden onset severe pain, redness and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the right foot that woke him at 4am. This is his first such episode and there is no preceding trauma. He has a history of a duodenal ulcer 3 years ago managed with proton pump inhibitor and is reluctant to take any NSAID; ibuprofen tried for this episode caused immediate epigastric pain.

On examination he is afebrile. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is exquisitely tender with overlying erythema, warmth and swelling extending to the dorsum of the foot. He cannot bear weight. There is no skin breach and no extension proximally. There are no tophi and no other inflamed joints. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 65 mL/min/1.73 m2 with a normal urinary albumin to creatinine ratio. Serum urate today is 0.48 mmol/L. CRP is 84 mg/L; FBC and LFTs are within normal limits. He is on no medications other than metformin 500 mg twice daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Right first MTP joint exquisitely tender, erythematous, warm, swollen; cannot weight bear; no tophi or other inflamed joints
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 65 mL/min/1.73 m2; urate 0.48 mmol/L; CRP 84 mg/L; FBC and LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Probenecid 500 mg twice daily orally as a uricosuric agent to lower serum urate concentration
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g pulse infusion over 60 minutes for severe inflammatory flare control
Indometacin 50 mg three times daily orally with a proton pump inhibitor cover for gastric protection
Oral colchicine 1 mg now then 500 micrograms 1 hour later, with maximum 1.5 mg in 24 hours
Allopurinol 100 mg orally daily commenced today as urate lowering therapy for prevention

stem:
A 65-year-old man with established stable angina diagnosed 3 years ago by exercise stress echocardiogram (single vessel left circumflex disease, non revascularisation candidate) reviews you for ongoing symptom control. He takes bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg and perindopril 4 mg. He is a former smoker (quit 4 years ago), is normotensive, and walks his dog daily but reports two episodes of central chest tightness per week on inclines that settle within 3 minutes of rest and use of glyceryl trinitrate spray.

On examination he is comfortable. Resting heart rate 58 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg. Heart sounds are dual with no murmur and the chest is clear. There is no peripheral oedema. He is in sinus rhythm on a recent ECG with no Q waves. A recent transthoracic echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular ejection fraction 60% with no valvular disease. A repeat exercise stress echocardiogram 3 months ago shows the same single vessel disease without progression. He is keen to remain functional and prefers to add medication rather than undergo angiography.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58/min, BP 124/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds dual, no murmur; chest clear; no peripheral oedema; sinus rhythm
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: LVEF 60%, no valvular disease; recent stress echo: single vessel left circumflex disease without progression
data_table.Medications: Bisoprolol 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg, perindopril 4 mg, GTN spray PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next addition?

options.text: Add nicorandil 10 mg orally twice daily as a potassium channel opener with nitrate like action
Add diltiazem 60 mg orally three times daily as a non dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Refer for coronary angiography with consideration of percutaneous coronary intervention for revascularisation
Add ranolazine 500 mg orally twice daily as a late sodium current inhibitor for refractory symptoms
Add amlodipine 5 mg orally daily as a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for anti anginal benefit

stem:
A 45-year-old woman with newly diagnosed primary hypothyroidism reviews you in your general practice 8 weeks after starting levothyroxine 50 mcg daily. Her diagnosis was made on a TSH of 28 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and a free T4 of 7 pmol/L (10 to 22), with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. She weighs 65 kg, has no cardiovascular disease, and is not pregnant. Initial fatigue and cold intolerance have improved but she still notes mild fatigue at the end of the day.

She has been taking her levothyroxine each morning on an empty stomach 30 minutes before breakfast and coffee, with no calcium, iron, or proton pump inhibitor co administration. Compliance has been complete according to the pharmacy records. She is on no other regular medications. Today's blood pressure is 122/74 mmHg, pulse is 68 in sinus rhythm and she is clinically euthyroid on examination. The latest thyroid panel reports TSH 12.5 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 12 pmol/L (10 to 22) and free T3 within normal limits. Other biochemistry is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Clinically euthyroid; no goitre; no tremor
data_table.Investigations: TSH 12.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); free T4 12 pmol/L (10-22); free T3 within normal limits; weight 65 kg
data_table.Medications: Levothyroxine 50 mcg daily for 8 weeks taken correctly on empty stomach

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase levothyroxine to 75 mcg orally each morning and repeat the TSH in 6 to 8 weeks
Add liothyronine 10 mcg orally daily as combination therapy for residual fatigue symptoms
Continue current 50 mcg dose and repeat thyroid function tests in 6 months as a stable dose
Increase to 100 mcg orally each morning and repeat thyroid function tests in 4 weeks
Switch to natural desiccated thyroid extract 60 mg orally daily as an alternative replacement formulation

stem:
A 48-year-old plumber is referred to the endocrinology clinic by his general practitioner with a 12 month history of progressive change in his appearance. He has noticed that his wedding ring no longer fits, his shoes have gone from size 10 to size 12, and his glove size has gone up. He has new daily frontal headaches, oily skin and sweating that disturbs his sleep. His wife noted his lower jaw has become more prominent in a recent family photograph compared with one from 5 years ago.

On examination he has coarse facial features with prominent supraorbital ridges and prognathism. His tongue is enlarged. Hand examination reveals spade-like fingers with skin tag development. Blood pressure is 158/95 mmHg. There is no visual field defect on confrontation. Cardiac and respiratory examination are unremarkable. Random growth hormone concentration done by the referring doctor was 6 mcg/L (under 1 in healthy adults); insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is markedly elevated for his age and sex. Renal function is normal and HbA1c is 7.2%. A pituitary MRI has been requested but not yet performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 158/95 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse facial features with prominent supraorbital ridges and prognathism; enlarged tongue; spade-like fingers; visual fields full on confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Random GH 6 mcg/L (<1 healthy); IGF-1 markedly elevated for age and sex; HbA1c 7.2%; renal function within normal limits; MRI pituitary not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Random morning cortisol and TSH to screen for combined pituitary hormone abnormalities first
Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurements at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes
24-hour urinary insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) measurement to confirm overproduction objectively
Insulin tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurements during induced hypoglycaemia
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with contrast as the first definitive confirmatory investigation

stem:
A 68-year-old man is referred to your acute medical clinic with 6 months of progressive mid-thoracic back pain, intermittent fatigue and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. He has no fever, night sweats or lymphadenopathy. He worked as a builder until retirement 3 years ago. There has been no recent travel and no obvious infective history. He has been managing the back pain with paracetamol with limited benefit and the general practitioner has organised initial bloods.

On examination he is pale. Cardiac and respiratory examination is unremarkable. There is tenderness over the thoracic spine at T8 with no neurological deficit in the lower limbs. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. Initial bloodwork shows haemoglobin 92 g/L, white cell count 6.2 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 218 x10^9/L. Creatinine has risen from 90 (3 years ago) to 168 micromol/L. Corrected calcium is 2.85 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60). Albumin is 32 g/L. ESR is 110 mm/hour. LFTs and TSH are within normal limits. The general practitioner has organised a thoracic spine X-ray which shows multiple lytic lesions in T7 and T8 vertebral bodies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 132/80 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, T8 thoracic tenderness, no neurological deficit; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, WCC 6.2 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 218 x10^9/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (was 90 three years ago); corrected calcium 2.85 mmol/L; albumin 32 g/L; ESR 110 mm/hour; LFTs and TSH within normal limits; thoracic spine: lytic lesions T7 and T8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Whole body PET-CT to exclude other haematological malignancies and solid organ neoplasm as differential
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with flow cytometry as the first diagnostic procedure today
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chains and urinary Bence Jones protein
Renal biopsy to identify the cause of acute kidney injury and proteinuria before any further workup
Whole body magnetic resonance imaging to characterise the extent of skeletal disease across the axial skeleton

subtopic_detail: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis disease modifying therapy
stem:
A 70-year-old retired farmer is referred to your respiratory clinic with 18 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and a daily dry cough. He has been previously well, is a never smoker, and has no occupational asbestos history despite his farming background. He has no current bird exposure, no humidifier use, and a recent normal echocardiogram with no pulmonary hypertension. He has no joint or skin features of connective tissue disease, and the rheumatology screen ordered by his general practitioner including ANA, ENA, RF, anti-CCP and myositis panel is negative.

On examination he is comfortable at rest with no clubbing. There are bilateral basal fine end-inspiratory velcro crackles to mid zone on auscultation. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. High resolution computed tomography of the chest is reported by the multidisciplinary meeting as showing peripheral and basal predominant honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, and reticulation; no ground glass, no nodules and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 65% predicted, FEV1/FVC 80%, DLCO 50% predicted. The MDM has reached a confident diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest, no clubbing; bilateral basal fine end-inspiratory crackles
data_table.Investigations: HRCT: peripheral basal honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, reticulation, no ground glass; PFT: FVC 65% predicted, DLCO 50% predicted; rheumatology screen negative; echocardiogram no PH
data_table.MDM: Multidisciplinary diagnosis: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (definite UIP pattern)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disease modifying treatment?

options.text: Oral N-acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily as a mucolytic and antioxidant for disease modification
Pulse intravenous cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m2 monthly as immunosuppressive induction for 6 months
Mycophenolate mofetil 1 g orally twice daily with regular full blood count and LFT monitoring
Oral pirfenidone titrated to 801 mg three times daily with photosensitivity precautions and LFT monitoring
Long-term oral prednisolone 30 mg daily with calcium and vitamin D for bone protection and azithromycin prophylaxis

stem:
A 56-year-old woman is referred to your general medicine clinic with a 4-month history of episodic flushing of the upper chest and neck, watery diarrhoea up to 8 times daily, and audible wheeze with intermittent dyspnoea during the flushing attacks. She has lost 5 kg of weight. Her primary care general practitioner organised a transthoracic echocardiogram for the wheeze; it shows tricuspid valve leaflet thickening with severe regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis, with preserved left ventricular function.

On examination she has a slightly cyanotic facial complexion. There is no telangiectasia. JVP is mildly elevated with a giant V wave. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge augmenting with inspiration. Abdomen is soft with mild right upper quadrant fullness; bowel sounds are active. There is no obvious lymphadenopathy. CT abdomen and pelvis ordered as part of her weight loss workup shows a 2 cm enhancing mass in the terminal ileum, multiple bilobar liver lesions and mild mesenteric desmoplastic reaction. Liver function tests are within normal limits today; renal function and electrolytes are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild facial cyanosis; JVP elevated with giant V wave; lower left sternal edge pansystolic murmur augmenting with inspiration; RUQ fullness
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: tricuspid leaflet thickening with severe regurgitation, pulmonary stenosis, preserved LV function; CT abdomen: 2 cm enhancing terminal ileal mass, multiple bilobar liver lesions, mesenteric desmoplasia; LFTs, renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Plasma chromogranin A measurement and serum serotonin measurement as ambulatory screening biomarkers
Image guided percutaneous liver biopsy of the largest lesion under ultrasound guidance for histology
Iodine-131 metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan for catecholamine-secreting tumour imaging
68-Ga DOTATATE positron emission tomography for tumour somatostatin receptor expression mapping
24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid measurement on a low amine diet for 2 consecutive collections

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection rate control before vasodilator
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a tertiary ED. A 58-year-old previously well man presents with sudden severe interscapular pain radiating to his lower back that began 90 minutes ago while walking. He is on no regular medications and has no past medical history beyond untreated hypertension. He smokes 20 per day. CT aortogram has confirmed a type B aortic dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery with no end-organ ischaemia and no rupture.

On examination he is restless and uncomfortable but cooperating. He has equal radial pulses, neurologically intact lower limbs, and a soft non-tender abdomen. He has no clinical signs of cardiac tamponade. The vascular surgeon has been consulted and recommends initial medical management. The intensive care team is preparing a bed and the consultant cardiologist has been informed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 105/min, BP 196/118 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Restless, cooperating; equal radial pulses; abdomen soft, non-tender; lower limbs warm with intact pulses and sensation
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, no ischaemic changes; troponin 8 ng/L (under 14); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial intravenous therapy?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion alone targeting mean arterial pressure under 80
Intravenous sodium nitroprusside infusion immediately to drop systolic BP under 120
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion as the first-line vasodilator titrated to BP
IV esmolol or labetalol to HR <60 first, then add IV vasodilator (GTN or nicardipine) for BP
Oral metoprolol 50 mg plus oral amlodipine 5 mg as adequate initial control

subtopic_detail: Resuming heart failure drugs after an admission with hyperkalaemia
stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction was admitted a week ago with hyperkalaemia during an episode of gastroenteritis. Perindopril and spironolactone were both stopped. He is euvolaemic and well in clinic today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.4 mmol/L; creatinine 118 micromol/L, back to baseline; eGFR 55 mL/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart perindopril at a reduced dose with early review
Restart both agents at their previous doses today
Leave both agents ceased and increase the furosemide
Leave both agents ceased and add a beta blocker today
Restart spironolactone alone at a reduced dose with review

subtopic_detail: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia hypertonic saline bolus
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a tertiary ED reviewing a 78-year-old woman commenced on sertraline 50 mg daily and amitriptyline 25 mg nocte 2 weeks ago for depression and chronic pain. She was found by her daughter having a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds with post-ictal drowsiness. She has no other medical history of note and was previously well. She has not been drinking excessive fluid.

On examination she is post-ictal but rousable to voice. She is clinically euvolaemic with normal jugular venous pressure, no peripheral oedema, and warm peripheries. Cortisol and TSH are within range. She has no clinical evidence of heart failure, cirrhosis, or hypovolaemia. The renal team and intensive care team are aware and a HDU bed is being prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 120/70 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal but rousable; euvolaemic; chest clear; abdomen soft; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 112 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.8 mmol/L; urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, plasma osmolality 248 mOsm/kg; urine Na 65 mmol/L; cortisol within range; TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: IV 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 10 minutes, repeat to raise Na 4-6 mmol/L
Intravenous 0.9% saline at 250 mL/hour with daily sodium monitoring
Fluid restriction to 500 mL/day alone with repeat sodium in 12 hours
Intravenous tolvaptan 30 mg as a vasopressin receptor antagonist infusion
Intravenous mannitol 25 g infusion for presumed cerebral oedema management

stem:
You are the medical registrar in a regional ED reviewing a 52-year-old woman with long-standing primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone 10 mg morning, 5 mg lunch, 5 mg evening, and fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. She has had 24 hours of vomiting from a presumed gastroenteritis and was unable to keep her medications down today. She has presented to the ED feeling weak, dizzy, and confused.

On examination she is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13. Her peripheries are cool and her capillary refill is 3 seconds. She has no fever and no focal infection on examination. She has had no recent surgery or other intercurrent illness. The endocrine team is on the way but you are managing the acute resuscitation. The HDU bed has been requested.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13; cool peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds; mucous membranes dry; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Na 126 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); glucose 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90); cortisol pending; venous gas pH 7.30

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous ondansetron 4 mg and oral rehydration salt trial over 2 hours
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg plus 0.9% saline 1 L bolus and dextrose if hypoglycaemic
Intravenous fludrocortisone 200 mcg as the primary mineralocorticoid replacement
Oral hydrocortisone 50 mg with intravenous fluids only and no IV glucocorticoid
Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg as preferred glucocorticoid in adrenal crisis

stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 30-year-old woman in your suburban clinic after she was stung by a bee on her arm 8 minutes ago in the waiting room. She has no prior allergy history but has developed generalised urticaria, marked lip and tongue swelling, hoarse voice, audible stridor, and an audible wheeze over the past 5 minutes. She feels dizzy on standing.

On examination she is anxious and unable to complete sentences. The practice nurse has placed her supine on the floor, has cannulated her, and has the emergency drug box open. An ambulance has been called and is 8 minutes away. The practice has IM and IV adrenaline available in standard ampoules of 1:1000 strength. There is no anaphylaxis action plan on file.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 80/52 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Anxious, sentence fragments only; generalised urticaria; lip and tongue swelling; stridor at rest; bilateral wheeze; capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 6.4 mmol/L; no other bedside investigations available; cannula in situ

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 100 mcg bolus given via the peripheral cannula
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 as the primary therapy for stridor
Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral mid-thigh
Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg first while preparing adrenaline
Intravenous promethazine 25 mg to reduce histamine-mediated effects

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation with TXA timing
stem:
You are the trauma team registrar in a tertiary trauma centre when a 28-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He is hypotensive despite 1 L of crystalloid given by ambulance, with a rigid abdomen on examination and a clinically unstable pelvic fracture. His Glasgow Coma Scale is 12. FAST scan is positive in the right upper quadrant and pelvis.

On arrival the airway is intact and he is breathing spontaneously. He has 2 large bore cannulae and a third intraosseous in his left tibia. Group and hold has been sent and the blood bank has been called. The general surgery and orthopaedics teams have been activated and theatre is being prepared. The trauma consultant is leading the resuscitation and asks you to direct the next blood product and pharmacological intervention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, cool peripheries; rigid abdomen; clinically unstable pelvis on gentle compression (no springing); GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (130-170); lactate 5.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); base excess -8 mmol/L; INR 1.4; fibrinogen 1.5 g/L (1.5-4.0); platelets 110 x10^9/L; FAST positive RUQ and pelvis

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: 4 units of packed red blood cells plus 4 units of fresh frozen plasma given over 2 hours
Packed red blood cells alone plus crystalloid until INR confirms coagulopathy
Whole blood transfusion 4 units only as sole product, without ratio mix or TXA
Activate MTP at 1:1:1 ratio of PRBC:FFP:platelets plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 min
Recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms/kg as initial haemostatic adjunct

stem:
You are the ED registrar in a tertiary trauma centre as a 24-year-old man arrives 20 minutes after a high-speed motorbike crash. He has blunt right-sided chest trauma and is in extreme respiratory distress on arrival. The paramedics report decreasing oxygen saturations and a falling blood pressure in transit. His airway is patent but he is using accessory muscles markedly.

On examination his trachea is deviated to the left, there are no breath sounds over the right hemithorax, and his right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion. His jugular venous pressure is raised at 8 cm. He is becoming progressively obtunded. There is no obvious open chest wound. A finger thoracostomy kit is at the bedside and the trauma consultant has just arrived.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 80/40 mmHg, RR 38/min, SpO2 89% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Distressed, drowsy; tracheal deviation to left; absent right-sided breath sounds; hyper-resonant right hemithorax; JVP raised at 8 cm
data_table.Investigations: No imaging performed (no time); ECG sinus tachycardia; no other bedside investigations

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate decompression site and follow-up?

options.text: 14G needle in 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line right, no follow-up tube needed
14 gauge needle in the xiphisternum for pericardiocentesis as primary intervention
Intercostal catheter at 5th ICS mid-axillary line first, before needle decompression
Bag-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen for 5 minutes then reassess thoracic
14G needle at 4th-5th ICS anterior axillary line right, then intercostal catheter

stem:
A 64-year-old man is reviewed in the orthopaedic ward 3 days after right total knee replacement. He has been on enoxaparin 40 mg daily as prophylaxis. He develops sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain over the past 30 minutes. He has no history of bleeding, no recent stroke, and no relevant family history.

On examination he is alert and oriented. He has tachypnoea, oxygen saturations of 88% on room air improving to 95% on 4 L by nasal prong. There are no signs of haemodynamic shock. The CTPA performed urgently shows a large saddle embolus with right ventricular dilation and a right-to-left ventricle diameter ratio greater than 1.0. There is no signs of overt cardiogenic shock and he remains awake and conversing throughout assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 105/72 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 95% on 4 L nasal prong, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild respiratory distress; clear chest auscultation; cardiac dual heart sounds no murmur; right calf swelling 2 cm greater than left circumference; no overt cardiogenic shock signs
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 95 ng/L (<14), BNP 850 pg/mL (<100); CTPA large saddle PE with RV dilation, RV:LV ratio >1.0; eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m²; INR 1.0, platelets 195 x10⁹/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion with HDU admission for close haemodynamic monitoring and cardiology and respiratory input, reserving systemic thrombolysis for haemodynamic deterioration

Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg infused over 2 hours immediately given the size of the saddle embolus and right ventricular dilation seen on the CT pulmonary angiogram performed in radiology
Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kg subcutaneously twice daily and ward admission for ongoing observation and serial troponin and BNP monitoring while continuing standard nursing observations

Catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy as definitive first-line therapy in the cath lab today, followed by therapeutic warfarin from day 1 with bridging heparin until INR is therapeutic over the next week
Insertion of inferior vena cava filter alone without anticoagulation given the recent surgery and possible bleeding concerns, with reassessment for anticoagulation start in 7 days postoperatively

subtopic_detail: Adult DKA - fluid first then insulin with potassium-led delay
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus (diagnosed age 11) presents to the emergency department with 12 hours of vomiting, polyuria, polydipsia and abdominal pain following a gastrointestinal viral illness. Her insulin pump dislodged 48 hours ago and she has not replaced the cannula. She weighs 65 kg.

On examination she is alert with Kussmaul respiration. Her mucous membranes are dry and capillary refill is 3 seconds. There is no focal abdominal tenderness or peritonism. Her bedside glucose is 28 mmol/L with serum ketones of 5.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.10, HCO3 10 mmol/L. Serum potassium is 5.4 mmol/L. She is haemodynamically compensated. She is fully oriented and her speech is coherent throughout the assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 28/min with Kussmaul respiration, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented; Kussmaul respiration; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; soft abdomen with mild diffuse tenderness; no peritonism; pump site erythematous
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 28 mmol/L (4-7); ketones 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6); pH 7.10, HCO3 10 mmol/L (22-26), anion gap 24; Na 134 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 110 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit per kilogram per hour immediately as the first intervention and add intravenous fluid resuscitation simultaneously as bicarbonate measurement results come back

Commence sodium chloride 0.9% 1 L over 1 hour as initial fluid resuscitation, then add intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit per kilogram per hour, with hourly potassium monitoring and replacement once below 5.5
Administer a bicarbonate infusion 100 mmol over 1 hour to correct the acidosis as the priority first intervention, followed by fluid resuscitation and insulin therapy once the pH normalises
Commence 10% dextrose infusion with subcutaneous intermediate acting insulin twice daily to address dehydration and provide background insulin while continuing oral rehydration with dietary salt

Trial of oral rehydration solution with subcutaneous rapid acting insulin 0.2 unit per kilogram and review in 4 hours given haemodynamic stability and ability to tolerate oral intake during this presentation

subtopic_detail: NSTEMI high GRACE score - early invasive within 24 hours
stem:
A 68-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and ex-smoker (20 pack-years) presents to the emergency department 4 hours after an episode of substernal chest discomfort lasting 30 minutes at rest, now resolved. He drove himself to hospital. He has no prior history of acute coronary syndrome and is on metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin.

On examination he is comfortable and pain free. There are no signs of heart failure or new murmur. His ECG on arrival shows 1 mm of ST depression in leads V4 to V6 with T wave inversion in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Troponin I drawn on arrival is 65 ng/L; repeat at 1 hour is 95 ng/L. His GRACE risk score in ED is 145. There is no history of bleeding and his estimated GFR is 65 mL/min/1.73 m².

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 135/85 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, pain free; no signs of heart failure; cardiac dual heart sounds no murmur; chest auscultation clear; peripheral pulses normal; no signs of bleeding diathesis
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 0 h 65 ng/L (<14), 1 h 95 ng/L; ECG ST depression V4-V6 plus T-wave inversion I/aVL/V5-V6; eGFR 65 mL/min/1.73 m²; haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180); HbA1c 8.0%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Conservative ischaemia-guided management with discharge after 24 hours of telemetry observation if asymptomatic and serial troponins down trending, with outpatient stress test arranged within 2 weeks

Immediate primary percutaneous coronary intervention within 90 minutes of arrival as if this were ST elevation myocardial infarction given the troponin rise and chest pain history at rest in this patient
Aspirin 300 mg loading dose plus ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose plus fondaparinux 2.5 mg subcutaneously plus cardiology admission with invasive coronary angiography within 24 hours of arrival

Thrombolysis with tenecteplase weight adjusted intravenous bolus dose given immediately as if this were ST elevation infarction, with subsequent transfer to a tertiary cardiology centre for ongoing care

Outpatient CT coronary angiography in 4 weeks with cardiology clinic review, with discharge today on aspirin only given the chest pain has resolved and ECG changes are non-specific in their distribution

subtopic_detail: Tumour lysis syndrome - rasburicase and hypocalcaemia management
stem:
A 32-year-old man newly diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma was admitted 36 hours ago to commence chemotherapy. Pre-chemotherapy bloods (baseline) were: K 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urate 480 micromol/L (200-420), phosphate 1.4 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.10-2.55) corrected, creatinine 95 micromol/L (45-90), LDH 1200 U/L (<250), estimated GFR 75 mL/min/1.73 m². He was started on allopurinol 300 mg orally daily and IV maintenance fluids 24 hours before chemotherapy.

12 hours after first dose of rituximab plus cyclophosphamide: K 6.1 mmol/L, urate 720 micromol/L, phosphate 2.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), corrected calcium 1.85 mmol/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L, LDH 2400 U/L. Urine output is 30 mL/h. ECG shows no peaked T waves and no QRS widening. G6PD assay sent 24 hours ago is still pending. He is asymptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 130/80 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
