data_table.Examination: Alert, comfortable; no Chvostek or Trousseau; no arrhythmia on monitor; no peripheral oedema; urine output 30 mL/h over past 4 hours
data_table.Investigations: K 6.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urate 720 micromol/L (200-420), phosphate 2.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), corrected calcium 1.85 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), creatinine 145 micromol/L (45-90), LDH 2400 U/L (<250); G6PD assay pending; ECG no peaked T or QRS widening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Maintenance fluids and oral allopurinol 300 mg daily with biochemistry recheck after 24 hours of chemotherapy completion and dietary phosphate restriction overnight on the haematology ward
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% to correct hypocalcaemia immediately with continued intravenous maintenance fluids and oral allopurinol therapy and recheck in 6 hours overnight
Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinise urine and oral allopurinol 600 mg daily with maintenance fluids and dietary potassium restriction to prevent further potassium rise overnight on the ward
IV 0.9% sodium chloride targeting urine output 100 mL per hour, single dose rasburicase 0.2 mg per kg IV, frequent biochemistry, and renal-replacement therapy if refractory to medical management

Withhold rasburicase pending G6PD assay result, continue allopurinol 600 mg daily, start sodium bicarbonate infusion to aid uric acid clearance and continue regular monitoring overnight on the haematology ward

stem:
A 41-year-old woman is seen in the endocrine outpatient clinic with an 18-month history of progressive central weight gain (12 kg), facial fullness with persistent facial redness, easy bruising on her forearms, oligomenorrhoea, and proximal muscle weakness with difficulty climbing stairs. Two months ago she was newly diagnosed with hypertension (BP 165/100) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.2%). She is on no glucocorticoids and has no exogenous steroid exposure including inhaled, topical, or intra-articular.

On examination she has wide (2 cm) purple abdominal striae, supraclavicular fullness, and proximal muscle weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4/5 hip flexion bilaterally). Her potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0) and her random morning serum cortisol is 920 nmol/L (50-550 morning). She has not yet had any other endocrine investigations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 165/100 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Cushingoid appearance; central obesity, facial fullness with plethora; supraclavicular fullness; wide purple abdominal striae 2 cm; proximal weakness MRC 4 of 5 hip flexion bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), HbA1c 8.2%, random AM cortisol 920 nmol/L (morning 50-550); FBC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits; pregnancy test negative; no exogenous steroid exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line investigation strategy?

options.text: Pituitary MRI with contrast immediately as the first investigation, then proceed to biochemical workup only if a pituitary mass is identified on the imaging study and refer to neurosurgery
Short Synacthen test 250 mcg with serum cortisol at baseline 30 minutes and 60 minutes to assess adrenal cortisol production response capacity over the standard testing interval used clinically
Random serum ACTH alone with serum cortisol at the time of sampling, taken at a single time point in the morning of clinic review, for interpretation against a normal range provided by the laboratory

Plasma renin to aldosterone ratio and saline suppression test for primary hyperaldosteronism workup as the priority investigation given the hypertension and hypokalaemia features that have developed recently

1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test and 24 hour urinary free cortisol as first-line screening, with plasma ACTH measurement once two of three screening tests confirm hypercortisolism over the next week

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation DOAC choice with renal impairment
stem:
A 78-year-old woman is reviewed by her GP for ongoing care of newly diagnosed non-valvular atrial fibrillation. She has a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease. She weighs 58 kg. She has had no falls or significant bleeding. She lives independently with her husband and remains mobile. Her HAS-BLED score is 2 and her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5 (age, hypertension, diabetes, female sex, T2DM).

She is currently on metformin 500 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and gliclazide 60 mg modified release daily. She has no documented mitral stenosis, no mechanical valve, and her recent transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated normal left ventricular function with mild mitral annular calcification. She is reviewed for choice of stroke prevention. Her eGFR has been stable at 32-34 mL/min/1.73m2 over the past 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min irregular, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no carotid bruit, no lower limb oedema; weight 58 kg; mental state intact, normal gait, no recent falls
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation; creatinine 138 micromol/L (50-90), eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m2; haemoglobin 124 g/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L; INR 1.0; transthoracic echo normal LV function with mild MAC; CHA2DS2-VASc 5, HAS-BLED 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line anticoagulation choice for this patient?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily orally as direct oral anticoagulation for non-valvular atrial fibrillation given her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5 and HAS-BLED is acceptable at 2
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily orally as direct oral anticoagulation for non-valvular atrial fibrillation given her renal function and age and weight profile
Dabigatran 110 mg twice daily orally as direct oral anticoagulation for non-valvular atrial fibrillation given her chronic kidney disease and age and stable eGFR
Warfarin titrated to INR 2 to 3 with weekly monitoring during initiation and monthly INR monitoring thereafter via a community pharmacy or general practice clinic
Aspirin 100 mg daily as antiplatelet therapy for stroke prevention given her age and concerns about bleeding risk on full anticoagulation given her chronic kidney disease today

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes immediate management
stem:
A 67-year-old man with stage 4 CKD attends the emergency department with one day of muscle weakness and palpitations. His regular medications include enalapril 20 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and a recent 5 day course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole started 4 days ago by his GP for a presumed UTI. He has not changed his diet but his urine output has decreased over the last 48 hours.

On arrival he is alert but feels generally weak. Bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm at 56/min with peaked T waves in the chest leads, broadened QRS at 124 ms, and absent P waves in lead II. A point-of-care blood gas confirms severe hyperkalaemia. Calcium gluconate has been drawn up by the nurse. He has been put on continuous cardiac monitoring and 2 large-bore intravenous cannulae have been sited. He is haemodynamically stable. There is no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, generalised weakness, no focal neurology, no ascites; no pitting oedema; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care VBG potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 132 mmol/L, pH 7.28, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L; creatinine 396 micromol/L (baseline 220), eGFR 14 mL/min/1.73m2; venous glucose 6.4 mmol/L; ECG sinus bradycardia 56/min, peaked T waves V2-V5, QRS 124 ms, absent P waves lead II

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next intervention?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg via mask in 4 mL of normal saline as a beta-2 agonist to shift potassium intracellularly via stimulation of the sodium potassium ATPase pump
Intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose over 15 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly with bedside glucose monitoring every 30 minutes for 4 hours
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL slow push over 2 minutes to stabilise the cardiac myocyte membrane with cardiac monitoring during administration of the bolus
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Resonium) 30 g now and repeat every 4 hours until normokalaemia is achieved with daily monitoring of his electrolytes and renal function
Urgent renal replacement therapy via temporary central venous access at the nearest tertiary centre and ICU transfer with nephrology consultation before any pharmacological intervention

subtopic_detail: Severe community acquired pneumonia AU empirical antibiotics
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 3 days of progressively worsening productive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, fever, and breathlessness. He is normally well, drinks 20 standard drinks per week, and smokes 15 cigarettes per day. He has not travelled recently and has no specific occupational exposures. He has no penicillin allergy.

On arrival he is alert but tachypnoeic with confusion to time on the AMTS (8 of 10). Bronchial breathing is heard at the right base with reduced expansion. Crackles extend up to mid zone. There is no peripheral oedema. A chest x-ray shows right middle and lower lobe consolidation with a small effusion. His SMART-COP score is calculated by the registrar including systolic blood pressure 88 mmHg, multilobar involvement, low albumin, respiratory rate 32, tachycardia 122, and confusion. He has had peripheral intravenous access established and 2 sets of blood cultures and a sputum sample have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 88/56 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breath sounds right base extending to mid zone with reduced expansion; small right pleural effusion; capillary refill 3 seconds; abbreviated mental test score 8 of 10
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP 312 mg/L (<5), urea 12.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); SMART-COP score 6 (very high); chest x-ray right middle/lower lobe consolidation with small effusion; blood cultures and sputum sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen to commence now?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly and intravenous doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly until microbiological results return and severity is reassessed
Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily as empirical cover for severe community-acquired pneumonia per Therapeutic Guidelines
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly and intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose as broad spectrum cover for severe pneumonia with possible MRSA
Intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily as monotherapy targeting Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical pathogens together with a single agent in severe community-acquired pneumonia
Oral amoxicillin 1 g 8-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days outpatient with telephone review in 48 hours from the GP for symptom progression

stem:
A 72-year-old man with stage 3a CKD, type 2 diabetes, and stable angina is admitted with new exertional chest pain. He is taking metformin 1 g twice daily, ramipril 10 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, perindopril, atorvastatin, and a recent course of ibuprofen for back pain. Troponin is mildly elevated and he has been booked for invasive coronary angiography in the morning.

He is haemodynamically stable. He is on a low background of oxygen 2 L/min for slight hypoxia. The cardiology team have asked you to prepare him for the procedure. His baseline creatinine is 138 micromol/L and his estimated GFR is 42 mL/min/1.73m2. Last echocardiogram showed normal LV function. He has had no recent diarrhoea, vomiting, or oral intake change. The procedure is non-emergent and could be delayed 24 hours if clinically warranted to optimise his renal status before exposure to iodinated contrast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on 2 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mucous membranes moist, no oedema; capillary refill 2 seconds; no focal cardiac findings beyond mild gallop rhythm; no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 9.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 138 micromol/L (50-90), eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m2; troponin I 78 ng/L (<14, normal less than 14); haemoglobin 124 g/L; HbA1c 7.8% (5.6-6.4%)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate prophylactic intervention to reduce his risk of contrast-induced acute kidney injury?

options.text: Intravenous isotonic 0.9% sodium chloride at 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre-procedure and 12 hours post-procedure with monitoring of fluid status and urine output
Oral N-acetylcysteine 600 mg twice daily for 24 hours pre-procedure and 24 hours post-procedure as a pharmacological prophylaxis for contrast-induced acute kidney injury
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 154 mmol/L at 3 mL/kg/hour for 1 hour pre-procedure and 1 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours post-procedure for renal protection against contrast nephropathy
Withhold metformin for 48 hours pre-procedure and 48 hours post-procedure to reduce the risk of lactic acidosis associated with metformin retention after iodinated contrast exposure
Pre-procedure furosemide 20 mg intravenously and mannitol 100 mL of 20% solution to maintain urine output during the procedure and post-procedure to reduce contrast nephropathy

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis precipitated by intercurrent illness
stem:
A 41-year-old man with primary adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune Addison disease, diagnosed 6 years ago) attends a metropolitan emergency department brought in by his wife. He has had 2 days of fever, profuse vomiting, and watery diarrhoea after a barbecue. He stopped his oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone 36 hours ago because of the vomiting. He has lost approximately 4 kg in body weight over this period and now feels too weak to stand.

On arrival he is lethargic but rousable. His mucous membranes are dry, capillary refill is 4 seconds, and he has flat neck veins on examination. There is a faint diffuse hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa and palmar creases. There is no abdominal tenderness or peritonism. He has known hypothyroidism on thyroxine 100 mcg daily. His usual hydrocortisone dose is 15 mg morning and 5 mg afternoon. He carries an emergency hydrocortisone vial but has not used it. He has not had any recent steroid dose adjustment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, flat neck veins, capillary refill 4 seconds; buccal and palmar crease hyperpigmentation; abdomen soft non-tender; no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 6.0 mmol/L, urea 14.8 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88); venous blood gas pH 7.30, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous glucose 3.2 mmol/L; cortisol pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus immediately followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous infusion or 50 mg 6-hourly with intravenous 0.9% saline resuscitation
Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg now to provide glucocorticoid replacement and allow the planned short synacthen test to remain interpretable for diagnostic confirmation
Intravenous fludrocortisone equivalent 1 mg orally or via nasogastric tube alongside aggressive fluid resuscitation with intravenous 0.9% saline at 1 L over the first hour
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL slow push for hyperkalaemia and then insulin-dextrose to shift potassium followed by intravenous hydrocortisone replacement at standard maintenance dose
Take blood and urine cultures and commence intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g empirically as the most likely cause of his decompensation given the fever and gastrointestinal infection symptoms today

subtopic_detail: Sgarbossa criteria in chest pain with new LBBB
stem:
A 64-year-old woman with hypertension and dyslipidaemia presents to a regional emergency department by ambulance with 80 minutes of severe central chest pain radiating to her left jaw and arm. She is sweaty and nauseated. There is no syncope and no cyanosis. She has a baseline ECG from 18 months ago in her electronic record which showed sinus rhythm with a normal QRS axis and no bundle branch block.

On arrival she is alert but in distress with the pain. Her bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with new left bundle branch block; in V1-V3 there is 3 mm concordant ST elevation, in lead III there is 2 mm discordant ST elevation, and in V6 there is 5 mm discordant ST depression. Her chest is clear; cardiovascular examination is otherwise unremarkable. There is no peripheral oedema. A point-of-care troponin returns at 22 ng/L (less than 14). The nearest PCI-capable centre is 80 minutes by road. She has been given aspirin 300 mg orally and clopidogrel 600 mg orally in the ambulance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pain at rest, diaphoretic; chest clear, dual heart sounds with soft S4 gallop; no peripheral oedema; capillary refill 2 seconds; carotid pulses equal and full
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm with new LBBB, V1-V3 with 3 mm concordant ST elevation, lead III with 2 mm discordant ST elevation, V6 with 5 mm discordant ST depression; troponin I 22 ng/L (<14); haemoglobin 134 g/L; chest x-ray clear; baseline ECG (18 months ago) sinus rhythm no BBB

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Repeat the ECG in 30 minutes after analgesia and another point-of-care troponin and only escalate to reperfusion therapy if the second troponin returns elevated above the threshold
Arrange direct transfer to the nearest percutaneous coronary intervention capable centre for primary PCI within 120 minutes from first medical contact regardless of the LBBB ECG findings
Commence intravenous heparin 60 units/kg loading and 12 units/kg/hour infusion plus high-dose statin pending serial 3 hour troponin and admit to the coronary care unit for medical management
Administer thrombolysis with tenecteplase based on weight and reassess for transfer to a PCI-capable centre if symptoms persist or ECG fails to improve within 60 to 90 minutes
Administer intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion and intravenous morphine for pain relief and observe the ECG response while transferring her to the cardiology ward for further evaluation

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department 26 hours after the start of a staggered paracetamol ingestion. She began taking the tablets at 6 pm yesterday and continued at intervals over an 11-hour period, finishing at 5 am today. She has taken her own count of 24 x 500 mg tablets (total 12 g over 11 hours). She has been crying and nauseated since the morning. She drinks heavily on weekends, around 6 standard drinks per night, and takes regular oral contraceptive pill.

She is alert and oriented. She has mild right upper quadrant tenderness but no peritonism. She is haemodynamically stable. Bedside venous blood gas shows a mild metabolic acidosis. She has no other co-ingestants on history; urine drug screen is pending. She admits to ongoing suicidal ideation. The toxicology service has been contacted by phone. Mental health team have been notified. Her weight is 65 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert oriented; mild right upper quadrant tenderness; no peritonism; no asterixis, no jaundice; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol level 95 mg/L (taken on arrival); ALT 1280 U/L (<35), AST 1140 U/L, INR 2.1, creatinine 88 micromol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous blood gas pH 7.32; urine bhCG negative; weight 65 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Do not start acetylcysteine because the paracetamol nomogram cannot be applied to staggered ingestions and the level falls below the standard 4 hour treatment line cut off
Arrange urgent liver transplantation assessment based on King's College Hospital criteria before commencing acetylcysteine to facilitate listing and avoid delay if she meets transplant criteria today
Administer single dose oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe for 4 hours with repeat paracetamol level to plot on the nomogram before commencing further definitive antidotal treatment
Discharge the patient with referral to community mental health team and the GP for further follow up since the paracetamol level of 95 mg/L is below the treatment threshold for acute single ingestion
Commence intravenous acetylcysteine using the 2 bag regimen with 200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours and refer to hepatology for King's College Hospital criteria assessment

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after first unprovoked PE
stem:
A 56-year-old previously well man was diagnosed with an unprovoked segmental pulmonary embolism three months ago after presenting with pleuritic chest pain and a CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrating filling defects in the right lower lobe segmental arteries. There was no recent surgery, hospitalisation, immobility, long-haul travel, malignancy, or hormonal therapy.

He was commenced on apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, and is now reviewed at the haematology clinic. He has had no bleeding, no recurrent symptoms, and tolerates the medication well. He has no family history of VTE. A thrombophilia screen was not performed. Renal function and platelet count are within normal limits. He asks how long he should continue treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no calf swelling, lungs clear, no signs of recurrent VTE
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: right lower lobe segmental PE; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; no thrombophilia screen performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from this review onwards?

options.text: Stop apixaban now; first unprovoked PE has reached the 3-month minimum duration
Continue apixaban at 5 mg twice daily for a further 3 months only
Continue extended apixaban at 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely given low bleed risk
Switch to warfarin with INR target 2 to 3 for extended secondary prevention regimen
Stop apixaban now and commence low-dose aspirin 100 mg daily for secondary prevention

stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred from primary care after a DEXA scan ordered for a fall demonstrated T-scores of -2.8 at the lumbar spine and -2.6 at the femoral neck. She had a minimal-trauma right wrist fracture six months ago when she slipped on wet pavement. Her FRAX 10-year hip fracture risk is calculated at 4 percent.

She takes no current medications, has no past gastrointestinal history, no malabsorption, and no malignancy. Renal function: creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR more than 90 mL/min/1.73 m2. Calcium and vitamin D were repleted three months ago and are within normal limits at 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (more than 50). She has good dentition with no recent dental work or planned extractions. She can sit upright comfortably for 30 minutes after waking.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no kyphosis, mild knee crepitus, no overt frailty features
data_table.Investigations: DEXA: T -2.8 spine, -2.6 femoral neck; FRAX hip 4%; creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR >90; 25-OH-D 78 nmol/L (>50); no dental issues

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Calcium 600 mg with vitamin D 1000 IU daily and weight-bearing exercise only
Raloxifene 60 mg daily orally with continuation of calcium and vitamin D background
Teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneously daily for severe osteoporosis treatment
Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly with calcium 600 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU daily
Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months instead of oral bisphosphonate

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment for symptomatic Parkinson's disease
stem:
A 72-year-old retired carpenter has been seeing his GP over the past 12 months with a slowly progressive resting tremor of the right hand and difficulty initiating movements. His handwriting has become small and cramped and his wife has noted reduced facial expressivity. He has had two minor falls in the past month.

On examination he has a 4 Hz pill-rolling tremor at rest in the right hand that abolishes on movement, cogwheel rigidity in the right elbow, and bradykinesia on finger-tapping testing. His gait is shuffling with reduced arm swing on the right and his pull test is mildly impaired. His mood is euthymic, MMSE is 28/30, postural blood pressure shows no significant orthostatic drop, eye movements are full, and there are no cerebellar signs. He has been formally diagnosed with idiopathic Parkinson's disease by a neurologist and asks about starting treatment to keep working in his shed.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: 4 Hz pill-rolling rest tremor right hand, cogwheel rigidity right elbow, bradykinesia, shuffling gait, MMSE 28/30, no orthostatic drop, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain demonstrated mild generalised atrophy; DAT-SPECT not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Selegiline 5 mg daily orally as monotherapy to preserve dopaminergic neurons
Amantadine 100 mg twice daily orally for resting tremor and bradykinesia symptoms
Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily as dopamine-agonist-first regimen for tremor
Anticholinergic benzatropine 1 mg twice daily oral therapy for resting tremor predominantly
Levodopa with carbidopa 50 mg / 12.5 mg three times daily, titrated to motor response

subtopic_detail: Modified Duke criteria for definite infective endocarditis
stem:
A 64-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 18 months ago presents with three weeks of low-grade fevers, anorexia, and night sweats. He had two recent dental cleanings without antibiotic prophylaxis. He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily and atorvastatin.

On examination temperature is 38.2 degrees Celsius, pulse 96, blood pressure 116 by 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur not previously documented. Splinter haemorrhages are present in three nail beds. Two of three peripheral blood-culture sets drawn 12 hours apart grow Streptococcus mitis. Transthoracic echocardiogram is technically limited but suggests a small mobile echo-density on the aortic valve. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirms a 9 mm vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 116/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: soft new early diastolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages in 3 nail beds, no Janeway lesions, no Osler nodes
data_table.Investigations: blood cultures: 2 of 3 sets grow S. mitis; TOE: 9 mm vegetation aortic prosthetic valve with mild AR; CRP 78 mg/L (<5); WCC 13.5 x10^9/L (4-11)

lead_in: What is the most accurate diagnostic classification of this case?

options.text: Definite IE on the basis of two major criteria (positive blood cultures plus echocardiographic evidence)
Possible IE; needs one further blood culture set to upgrade to definite IE diagnosis
Rejected IE because only two of three blood-culture sets are positive for typical organism
Definite IE on basis of one major plus three minor criteria from this case alone
Possible IE; PET-CT should be added before commencing empirical antibiotics on suspicion

subtopic_detail: Initial investigation of suspected Cushing's syndrome
stem:
A 44-year-old woman presents with 14 months of progressive central weight gain (10 kg), facial rounding, easy bruising, proximal weakness climbing stairs, and new hypertension diagnosed three months ago (current BP 162 by 98 mmHg on amlodipine 5 mg daily). She also reports oligomenorrhoea over the past year.

On examination BMI is 33 with truncal adiposity, dorsocervical fullness, abdominal striae more than 1 cm wide and purplish in colour, and proximal weakness on sit-to-stand testing. She takes no exogenous glucocorticoids, no inhaled corticosteroids, no topical steroids, and no other medications other than amlodipine. Fasting glucose is 7.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), HbA1c 47 mmol/mol (less than 42), and potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). She drinks 2 standard drinks of wine per week and does not work shifts.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/98 mmHg, otherwise within normal limits
data_table.Examination: BMI 33 with truncal adiposity, dorsocervical fullness, wide purplish abdominal striae, proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: fasting glucose 7.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), HbA1c 47 mmol/mol (<42), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); no exogenous glucocorticoid exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line diagnostic test?

options.text: Random morning serum cortisol level taken at 0800 in the outpatient pathology clinic
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with 0800 cortisol the next morning
Plasma ACTH measurement at 0900 to distinguish ACTH-dependent from independent disease
MRI pituitary with gadolinium to look for a microadenoma at the corticotroph site
Random plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio with concurrent serum potassium replacement

subtopic_detail: Acute uncomplicated type B aortic dissection
stem:
A 62-year-old man with a 30-year history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe interscapular pain that began three hours ago while sitting at his desk. The pain is described as a tearing sensation. He took his usual amlodipine and irbesartan this morning.

On examination he is in obvious discomfort. Pulse 92 (regular), blood pressure 196 by 112 mmHg in the right arm and 188 by 108 mmHg in the left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Bilateral radial pulses are present and equal. Cardiac auscultation reveals no murmur, with normal first and second heart sounds. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, peripheral pulses are present in both lower limbs, and neurological examination is normal. CT angiography of the aorta shows an intimal flap commencing distal to the left subclavian artery and extending to the level of the renal arteries without branch-vessel compromise.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP right 196/112 mmHg left 188/108 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: equal radial pulses, no murmur, peripheral pulses present, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: CTA aorta: intimal flap from distal to L subclavian to renal arteries; no branch-vessel compromise; troponin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate haemodynamic management?

options.text: Intravenous nitroprusside infusion titrated rapidly to systolic BP under 120 mmHg
Intravenous loop diuretic furosemide 40 mg with morphine 5 mg for analgesia
Intravenous labetalol infusion titrated to heart rate 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
Immediate transfer to operating theatre for endovascular stent graft repair (TEVAR)
Immediate cardiothoracic surgical consult for ascending aorta surgical replacement repair

subtopic_detail: Pituitary apoplexy with visual loss and hypopituitarism
stem:
A 56-year-old man with a known 2 cm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma (diagnosed 4 years ago, on watchful waiting) presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe retro-orbital headache 90 minutes ago, followed by nausea, vomiting, and progressive loss of vision in the temporal fields of both eyes. He also reports double vision when looking laterally.

On examination he is alert but distressed. Pulse 58, blood pressure 86 by 54 mmHg lying flat, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral temporal field defects on confrontation, left lateral rectus weakness, and a sluggish pupillary response on the left. Neck is supple. Bedside glucose is 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-7.7). Serum sodium is 128 mmol/L (135-145). His regular medications include atorvastatin and irbesartan, no glucocorticoids. He has not been unwell otherwise.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 58, BP 86/54 lying flat, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, bilateral temporal field defects, left lateral rectus weakness, sluggish left pupil, neck supple
data_table.Investigations: bedside glucose 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), known 2 cm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma 4 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Urgent neurosurgical consult and transfer for transsphenoidal decompression first
MRI pituitary with contrast to confirm apoplexy before any pharmacological treatment
Intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus for hyponatraemia correction first
Intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg over 20 minutes to reduce intracranial pressure first
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, IV saline, then urgent neurosurgical referral and MRI

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection diagnosis and urgent intervention
stem:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin presents to the emergency department with a 36-hour history of rapidly worsening pain in his right thigh, three days after a minor scratch from gardening. The pain is now described as out of proportion to what he can see on the skin surface.

On examination he is pale, with pulse 132, blood pressure 90 by 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius. There is a 15 cm area of dusky, mottled skin over the anterior thigh with bullous changes at one edge, exquisite tenderness extending well beyond the visible erythema, and crepitus on palpation. Plain X-ray of the thigh shows scattered subcutaneous gas. Bloods: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 240 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 14 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), haemoglobin 116 g/L (130-170), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2). The calculated LRINEC score is 9.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 90/58, RR 28, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: 15 cm dusky mottled skin with bullae, exquisite tenderness beyond erythema, crepitus on palpation, pale and unwell
data_table.Investigations: X-ray thigh: scattered subcutaneous gas; WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 240 mg/L (<5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 14 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), Hb 116 g/L (130-170), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (<2); LRINEC score 9

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate priority?

options.text: Urgent surgical debridement in operating theatre with broad-spectrum antibiotics
MRI of the right thigh urgently to confirm necrotising fasciitis before theatre
Empirical IV flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly and reassess clinically in two hours of observation
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy referral as primary intervention before surgical debridement
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with crystalloid 30 mL/kg targeting MAP at least 65 mmHg first

stem:
A 34-year-old non-pregnant woman presents to the emergency department with two days of fevers, rigors, and right-sided loin pain on a background of dysuria and frequency for four days. She is otherwise well, has no allergies, has no urinary tract abnormalities, and is not catheterised. She is sexually active with a male partner and uses condoms; she had a uncomplicated cystitis 14 months ago treated with trimethoprim.

On examination she is unwell but not septic. There is marked right costovertebral angle tenderness. The abdomen is otherwise soft. She is tolerating oral fluids and food.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: right costovertebral angle tenderness, soft abdomen, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: urine dipstick: leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+; FBC WCC 14.6 x10^9/L; CRP 88 mg/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; lactate 1.8 mmol/L; urine culture and blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days at home
IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once-daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six hourly
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 14 days as outpatient therapy
IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg twelve hourly
IV meropenem 1 g eight hourly as the empirical first-line agent

stem:
A 68-year-old man with COPD reviews at your respiratory clinic. He has a 50 pack-year history (quit 4 years ago), GOLD group B disease, FEV1 56% predicted post-bronchodilator, and has been on tiotropium 18 micrograms daily for two years. In the past year he has had three moderate exacerbations requiring oral prednisolone and antibiotics, none requiring hospital admission. His mMRC dyspnoea grade is 3.

His blood eosinophil count is 380 cells per microlitre on a recent FBC. He has had no pneumonias. He uses his short-acting salbutamol inhaler about four times a week. He is on optimal non-pharmacological therapy (pulmonary rehabilitation completed, influenza and pneumococcal vaccines up to date, smoking cessation maintained).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: barrel chest, reduced air entry bilaterally, no wheeze at rest, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: FEV1/FVC 0.58 post-bronchodilator; FEV1 56% predicted; blood eosinophils 380 cells per microlitre

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in inhaled therapy?

options.text: Add oral azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly as long-term prophylaxis
Add a LABA to the LAMA but defer ICS until further exacerbations
Escalate to a LAMA plus LABA plus inhaled corticosteroid triple inhaler
Add oral theophylline 200 mg twice daily and review symptoms in 4 weeks
Stop tiotropium and switch to inhaled corticosteroid monotherapy

stem:
A 78-year-old woman is seen in your general practice with a new diagnosis of persistent atrial fibrillation, picked up on routine ECG when she presented with palpitations. She has hypertension on perindopril and amlodipine, type 2 diabetes on metformin, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a (eGFR 52 mL/min per 1.73 m^2). She has never had a stroke or TIA. She lives independently and has no falls history.

Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 4 (hypertension, age 75 or over, diabetes, female sex). HAS-BLED is 1 (hypertension). She has no contraindications to oral anticoagulation. She is rate-controlled on metoprolol 50 mg twice daily and has chosen a rate-control strategy after counselling.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: irregularly irregular pulse, no carotid bruits, no peripheral oedema, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: creatinine 102 micromol/L (45 to 90); eGFR 52 mL/min per 1.73 m^2; FBC and LFT within normal limits; ECG confirms AF rate 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulant choice?

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily orally for stroke prevention
Aspirin 100 mg daily as antiplatelet stroke prevention monotherapy
Warfarin titrated to a therapeutic INR of 2.0 to 3.0
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily orally indefinitely for stroke prevention
Left atrial appendage closure with a Watchman device alone

subtopic_detail: Monitoring for hypoglycaemia after insulin and dextrose are given
stem: A 71-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease was treated thirty minutes ago for hyperkalaemia with intravenous calcium, then insulin with dextrose. She is alert and her rhythm has normalised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 5.8 mmol/L; capillary glucose 7.4 mmol/L; creatinine 210 micromol/L

lead_in: What monitoring is most appropriate now?

options.text: Hourly capillary glucose for the next six hours
Capillary glucose once before the evening meal today
Venous glucose with the morning blood tests tomorrow
Hourly blood pressure alone while she remains alert
No further glucose testing as dextrose was given

stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department late at night with worsening left lower leg pain over 18 hours. He gave himself a small cut while gardening yesterday. The pain is now out of proportion to the small wound and he is reluctant to move his foot. He has had rigors at home and one episode of vomiting.

On examination there is a 1 cm puncture wound on the calf with surrounding erythema. The skin overlying the lateral calf is dusky purple in one area and tender well beyond the visible margin of erythema. There are no crepitations on palpation; an early plain film shows no gas. He is unwell-looking and rigoring on the trolley.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: pain out of proportion, dusky discolouration of skin lateral calf, tenderness beyond erythema margin, no crepitations
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L; haemoglobin 130 g/L (130 to 170); sodium 132 mmol/L; creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 80); CRP 240 mg/L; glucose 18.4 mmol/L; lactate 4.8 mmol/L; LRINEC score 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for immediate operative debridement after blood cultures and IV antibiotics
Mark the erythema with a marker pen and review in 4 hours on IV flucloxacillin
CT with contrast of the leg before any surgical referral to confirm the diagnosis
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy in addition to IV piperacillin-tazobactam, deferring surgery
Trial of IV flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly for 24 hours and reassess for debridement

stem:
A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with sudden-onset severe breathlessness and one episode of syncope at home 30 minutes ago. She returned from a long-haul flight three days ago. She has no past medical history of bleeding, no recent surgery, and is not on anticoagulants.

On arrival she is pale, cool peripherally, and clammy. The right ventricle is felt heaving on palpation of the lower sternum. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated and hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening. CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrates bilateral central filling defects. There is no evidence of intracranial pathology on CT brain and no history of recent stroke, surgery, or bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: cool peripheries, prominent neck veins, loud P2, no calf swelling, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: troponin I 220 ng/L (less than 14); BNP 1400 pg/mL; lactate 4.2 mmol/L; CTPA: bilateral central PE; echocardiography: dilated hypokinetic RV

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Emergent surgical pulmonary embolectomy as the first-line reperfusion strategy
Therapeutic enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg subcutaneously once daily and observe
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for outpatient management
IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours alongside resuscitation and unfractionated heparin
Inferior vena cava filter insertion before starting any anticoagulation

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with autoimmune Addison's disease is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, and confusion. She has been on hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg at lunchtime with fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily for 8 years. She has had a viral gastroenteritis for two days and stopped her hydrocortisone yesterday because she could not keep tablets down.

She is drowsy on arrival and disoriented to time and place. Her abdomen is diffusely tender without peritonism. She has been given 1 L of IV 0.9% sodium chloride en route. The medical registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 124 /min, blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy, dehydrated, abdomen mildly tender without peritonism, hyperpigmentation of buccal mucosa
data_table.Investigations: sodium 126 mmol/L (135 to 145); potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4); urea 12 mmol/L; creatinine 110 micromol/L (45 to 90)

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management step?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 20 mg stat once her vomiting has fully settled
IV dexamethasone 4 mg as a single dose while awaiting cortisol and ACTH results
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg as a bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours as a continuous infusion
IV fludrocortisone 200 micrograms with IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
Withhold steroids until a short Synacthen test confirms adrenal insufficiency

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with one hour of central crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw. He has hypertension and is a current smoker. Paramedics gave him aspirin 300 mg, oxygen, and sublingual GTN with one episode of profound hypotension after the GTN; his BP recovered with a 500 mL saline bolus.

On arrival he is pale and clammy but alert. The ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. A right-sided V4R lead shows 1.5 mm ST elevation. There is no murmur. Chest is clear and the JVP is elevated. Primary PCI is available on-site within 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 56 /min, blood pressure 92/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: elevated JVP, clear chest, no peripheral oedema, no murmurs
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 2 mm ST elevation II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression I/aVL; V4R 1.5 mm ST elevation; troponin I 380 ng/L (less than 14); chest film clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL bolus and prepare for primary PCI
IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion starting at 5 micrograms per minute
IV furosemide 40 mg now to offload the right ventricle today
IV metoprolol 5 mg now before transfer to the cardiac catheter lab
Fibrinolysis with tenecteplase as the primary reperfusion strategy

subtopic_detail: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura - avoid platelet transfusion
stem:
A 38-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with 4 days of fatigue, headache, and a petechial rash over her shins. She also describes intermittent visual disturbance for the last 24 hours. She has no recent infections, no medications, and no family history of bleeding.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 12 x 10^9/L, and white cells 7.6 x 10^9/L. Blood film shows numerous schistocytes (5 to 8 per high power field), polychromasia, and no blasts. LDH is 1280 U/L (less than 250), bilirubin 38 micromol/L (less than 20), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline unknown but eGFR estimated 42). Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Coagulation profile is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, oriented but mildly confused on detailed history, petechiae over shins, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no focal neurology, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-160), platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-450), schistocytes on film 5-8 per high power field, LDH 1280 U/L (under 250), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), DAT negative, creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90), coagulation profile normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discuss immediate plasma exchange with the haematology team and avoid platelet transfusion despite the platelet count
Transfuse a single adult dose of platelets to raise the platelet count above 50 x 10^9/L before any other intervention
Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for presumed sepsis-related microangiopathy syndromes
Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily as sole therapy and review response at the haematology ward round
Transfuse fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg as a substitute for plasma exchange while the exchange room is being prepared

stem:
A 62-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement four months ago is admitted to a tertiary cardiology unit with two weeks of fevers, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of 3 kg. He had a dental extraction six weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. He has no penicillin allergy and no intravenous drug use.

On examination he is alert but unwell-appearing. He has new conjunctival petechiae and three small painless lesions on the palms (Janeway lesions). Auscultation reveals an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a soft heart sound at the base. Capillary return is two seconds. Three separate sets of blood cultures over two hours have been collected. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a 9 mm vegetation on the aortic prosthesis with moderate aortic regurgitation but no abscess. His vital signs are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 124/64, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 102 g/L, white cells 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 162 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, three sets of blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for empirical native valve cover
Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours as monotherapy targeting methicillin sensitive staphylococcus aureus only
Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg load then 15 to 20 mg/kg twice daily, gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours, plus rifampicin
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for empirical Q fever endocarditis cover
Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours as broad spectrum empirical cover until culture results return

stem:
A 24-year-old male medical student presents to a metropolitan emergency department six hours after a hollow-bore needlestick injury sustained while clearing a sharps container. The source patient is a 38-year-old man known to be living with HIV; his most recent viral load three months ago was reported as undetectable on bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide and his HIV physician has been contactable.

The needle had visible fresh blood and entered the dorsum of the student's left hand to a depth of around 3 mm with active bleeding. The student washed the wound under running water and the injury was reported within 10 minutes. His baseline HIV serology, hepatitis B surface antibody (vaccinated, anti-HBs 240), hepatitis C antibody, and pregnancy considerations are not applicable. He has no current medications.

data_table.Investigations: source patient HIV viral load undetectable 3 months ago, source patient hepatitis B surface antigen negative, source patient hepatitis C antibody negative, student baseline HIV serology pending, anti-HBs 240 mIU/mL (>10 protective), student hepatitis C antibody pending, full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding HIV post exposure prophylaxis?

options.text: Reassure that the source undetectable viral load makes PEP unnecessary and arrange follow up serology at 6 weeks and 3 months
Commence 5 days of bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide and review at day 5 to decide whether to continue
Commence 28 days of zidovudine plus lamivudine as a two drug regimen following older Australian and overseas guidance
Commence 28 days of tenofovir 245 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, and raltegravir 400 mg twice daily within 72 hours of exposure
Defer PEP pending source patient viral load on the same day and start only if the result is detectable above 200 copies

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.4 percent on metformin and gliclazide) presents to a regional emergency department with 36 hours of progressive right calf pain and swelling after he caught his ankle on a fence post. The redness is now spreading rapidly above the knee. He says the pain is severe, much worse than the appearance suggests.

On examination he is unwell-appearing with rigors. The right calf is erythematous extending above the knee with a 12 cm patch of dusky purple skin, two small superficial blisters, and exquisite tenderness extending well beyond the visible margin of erythema. Sensation is reduced over part of the dusky area, and there is no crepitus. Vital signs are below. Bedside investigations are obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 124, blood pressure 102/62, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 124 g/L, white cells 22.4 x10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 17.4 mmol/L, creatinine 162 micromol/L, CRP 286 mg/L (<5), venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L, LRINEC score 9, plain radiograph of leg without subcutaneous gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Mark the leading edge of erythema, admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours, and review the leg in 12 hours
Administer high dose intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as the first intervention before surgical exploration of the leg
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours alone and arrange magnetic resonance imaging before any surgery
Apply hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the primary treatment without immediate surgical debridement by the on call surgical team
Take blood cultures, give intravenous meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin, and arrange urgent surgical debridement

stem:
A 64-year-old man with longstanding hypertension and bicuspid aortic valve known to a cardiologist presents to a regional emergency department with two hours of sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the interscapular area and now to the right loin. He says the pain was maximal at onset. He has not had recent trauma and has not used cocaine. He has had no syncope. He is a non-smoker.

On examination he is diaphoretic and frightened. The right radial pulse is weak; the left is normal. Right and left blood pressures differ by 28 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge that he says is new (last cardiology echo six months ago noted aortic regurgitation graded 'trivial'). There is no focal neurology, no abdominal tenderness, and palpable femoral pulses bilaterally. There is no clinical pneumothorax. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 188/96 right arm and 160/82 left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, troponin within normal limits, D-dimer 6.2 mg/L (<0.5), chest radiograph mediastinal widening, point-of-care echo dilated ascending aorta with intimal flap

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion targeting heart rate 60 to 80 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120, with immediate CT angiography
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 50 micrograms per minute to lower blood pressure as the priority intervention
Intravenous heparin 80 units/kg bolus then infusion for presumed pulmonary embolus given the markedly elevated D-dimer
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg with morphine 5 mg intravenously and admit for cardiac telemetry observation overnight
Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 90 minutes for suspected ST elevation myocardial infarction

stem:
A 36-year-old man is brought to the resuscitation bay of a major trauma centre 15 minutes after a high-speed motorcycle collision. He has bilateral femoral shaft fractures with active bleeding from the right thigh stump (a traumatic above-knee amputation), an open pelvic fracture, and a haemoperitoneum on focused ultrasound (FAST positive). He has had 1 unit of group O red cells from the trauma fridge en route.

On arrival he is alert but confused and pale. Pulse rate 142, blood pressure 76/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92 percent on 10 L oxygen via Hudson mask, temperature 35.4 degrees. Two large bore intravenous cannulae are in. The Code Crimson team has been activated. Initial bloods are returning. The trauma team consultant asks you to coordinate the haematology side of the resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 142, blood pressure 76/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92 percent on 10 L oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 64 g/L, platelets 122 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (2 to 4), lactate 6.8 mmol/L, base excess negative 8, ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L (1.10 to 1.30), ROTEM EXTEM CT 95 sec (38 to 79) and FIBTEM A10 6 mm (>10), shock index 1.9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give recombinant factor VII 90 micrograms/kg as the primary intervention to control bleeding before any other product
Transfuse two units of packed red cells, then reassess clinical status and laboratory results before further blood products
Give 2 L of crystalloid resuscitation before any blood products to restore peripheral perfusion and blood pressure
Activate the massive transfusion protocol at a 1:1:1 ratio with intravenous tranexamic acid, cryoprecipitate, and calcium
Defer tranexamic acid and rely on the trauma surgeon to achieve operative haemostasis before any antifibrinolytic agent

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with poorly adherent hypertension (intermittent perindopril and amlodipine over years) is brought to the emergency department with a 12 hour history of a generalised throbbing headache, two episodes of vomiting, and progressive blurred vision. She has noticed a yellow tinge to lights and difficulty reading texts. There is no focal weakness, no chest pain, and no dyspnoea.

On examination she is alert but uncomfortable. The optic discs are bilaterally swollen with retinal haemorrhages and cotton wool spots. Auscultation reveals mild bibasal crackles without overt fluid overload. Cardiac auscultation is normal. There is no abdominal aortic mass, no carotid bruit, and no focal neurology. Vital signs and bedside investigations are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 232/138, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead ECG sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, troponin within normal limits, urinalysis blood 2+ protein 2+, creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 92), CT brain within normal limits, chest radiograph mild pulmonary venous congestion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her blood pressure in the first hour?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 50 micrograms/min targeting a blood pressure under 140/90 within thirty minutes
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg and admit for cardiac telemetry observation with reassessment of blood pressure overnight
Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting mean arterial pressure reduction of about 20 percent over the first 60 minutes
Restart perindopril 5 mg and amlodipine 10 mg orally and review blood pressure response in twenty four hours' time
Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus repeated every 30 minutes targeting diastolic blood pressure under 70 mmHg today

subtopic_detail: Adrenal insufficiency and perioperative steroid cover
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) for 15 years on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg lunch, and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily is scheduled for an open Hartmann procedure for diverticular perforation under general anaesthesia. She arrives in the ED via ambulance hypotensive after one day of vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain. She missed her morning hydrocortisone today.

On arrival she is drowsy and pale. Capillary blood glucose 3.2 mmol/L. Pulse rate 132, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs, temperature 38.4 degrees. The abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness. CT shows free intraperitoneal air and free fluid consistent with perforated diverticulitis. The surgical team plans theatre as soon as she is stabilised. Bloods are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 132, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on 4 L oxygen, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, white cells 22.4 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 124 g/L, CT free intraperitoneal air, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours, saline resuscitation, antibiotics, and proceed to theatre
Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose, give intravenous fluids, and proceed to theatre once vital signs improve
Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg as the steroid of choice in adrenal crisis given its longer half life than hydrocortisone
Withhold steroids until a random cortisol level can be measured and a short Synacthen test arranged through endocrine
Intravenous fludrocortisone 200 micrograms as the priority before hydrocortisone for mineralocorticoid replacement now

subtopic_detail: Acute hyperkalaemia in chronic kidney disease
stem:
A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline eGFR 22) presents to a metropolitan emergency department with one day of generalised weakness and palpitations. His regular medications include ramipril 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg at night.

On examination he is alert with proximal muscle weakness limiting hip flexion. He is normotensive and not in fluid overload. ECG shows tall peaked T waves throughout the praecordial leads without QRS widening or P wave loss. Cardiac monitor confirms sinus rhythm. He has not had any vomiting, no recent gastroenteritis, no recent radiocontrast, and no over-the-counter medication changes. He took his usual morning dose of medications. He has no history of cardiac arrhythmia and no implanted device.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 78, blood pressure 142/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: potassium 7.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-28), creatinine 280 micromol/L (60-110), urea 22 mmol/L (3-8), eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m squared, glucose 8.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate sequence of management?

options.text: 10 percent calcium chloride 10 mL intravenously over 10 minutes then repeat urea and electrolytes at 30 minutes for trend assessment
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally and recheck the serum potassium in 4 hours for trend before any further intervention
Soluble insulin 10 units intravenously with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose intravenously over 30 minutes and observe for hypoglycaemia thereafter
Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously over 2 minutes, then insulin-dextrose and salbutamol nebuliser, and cease ramipril and spironolactone
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol intravenously over 5 minutes and arrange urgent haemodialysis with the on-call renal team for definitive treatment

subtopic_detail: Adult DKA initial fluid and insulin
stem:
A 25-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting, polyuria, and progressive lethargy following several days of viral upper respiratory illness. He has stopped his usual insulin glargine 20 units at night and his rapid-acting insulin doses for the past 24 hours because of vomiting and concerns about hypoglycaemia.

On examination he is alert with dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, and slow capillary return at three seconds. There is acetone on his breath and his respiration is deep and slow. He has no fever, no abdominal tenderness, and no localising signs of infection. His weight is 75 kg today. He has no chronic complications of diabetes and his HbA1c three months ago was 7.6 percent. There is no recent travel and no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 130, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.05, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L (22-28), glucose 32 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.0 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), urea 9 mmol/L (3-8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first hour of fluid and insulin management?

options.text: 1 litre 0.9 percent saline as a rapid bolus over 30 minutes then maintenance at 100 mL/hour without potassium replacement initially in the first hour
Insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately without prior fluid resuscitation and crystalloid only added once the potassium falls below 4.0 mmol/L
0.9 percent saline 1 L bolus over one hour with intramuscular insulin 10 units every 4 hours and oral potassium supplementation 2 grams daily
5 percent dextrose 1 L at 100 mL/hour and rapid-acting subcutaneous insulin 10 units stat with repeat doses every 2 hours guided by capillary glucose
0.9 percent saline 500 mL bolus over 15 to 30 minutes, reassess, then 250 to 500 mL/hour with insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour started after fluids are flowing

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with a long-standing history of asthma presents to a metropolitan emergency department with worsening shortness of breath over the past four hours. She is on long-acting beta-agonist and corticosteroid inhaler maintenance therapy. She has not had a hospital admission in the last 12 months but has needed three short oral prednisolone courses in the same period.

On arrival she is talking in single words, sitting upright with shoulder elevation. She has audible wheeze with use of accessory muscles. She has received three back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers (5 mg each) and one ipratropium nebuliser (500 micrograms) in the first 30 minutes. Peak expiratory flow is 35 percent of her best (380 L/min recorded six months ago). She has not yet received corticosteroid. She has no chest pain and no fever. Smoke detector activated cooking on her stove this morning.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 132, blood pressure 128/82, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 91 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.36, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, chest radiograph hyperinflated lung fields without consolidation or pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes plus intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg, continuous nebulised salbutamol, and senior medical review
Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1:1000 solution into the deltoid muscle and intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g for empirical antibacterial cover
Intravenous aminophylline loading dose 5 mg/kg over 30 minutes followed by a continuous infusion at 0.5 mg/kg/hour for ongoing bronchodilation
Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation in the emergency department resuscitation bay with paralysis and sedation
Heliox 70:30 helium-oxygen mixture by face mask as primary bronchodilator with continued back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers without further escalation

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary embolism Wells score and imaging strategy
stem:
A 72-year-old woman is reviewed on the orthopaedic ward on day 4 after an elective right total knee replacement. She is taking enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous prophylaxis. She has had four hours of sudden onset shortness of breath and right-sided pleuritic chest pain.

On examination she is mildly distressed with mild right calf swelling but no overt deep vein thrombosis signs. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are otherwise unremarkable with normal heart sounds and clear chest. Wells score is calculated: PE more likely than alternative diagnosis (3), HR over 100 (1.5), surgery in last 4 weeks (1.5), no haemoptysis, no malignancy, no previous PE; total score 6 (high probability). The on-call radiologist has called the intern to ask whether a D-dimer is required before CTPA is performed.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 110, blood pressure 124/74, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia rate 110 without S1Q3T3, chest radiograph clear lung fields without effusion or wedge, troponin within normal limits

lead_in: Which imaging strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Wait for D-dimer result with age-adjusted threshold of 0.72 mg/L (age multiplied by 0.01) and perform CTPA only if above this threshold to limit ionising radiation
Proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiogram without D-dimer because PE likely (Wells > 4) requires imaging-based exclusion regardless of D-dimer result
Perform ventilation-perfusion scan instead of CT pulmonary angiogram given the moderate-to-high pretest probability and current chronic kidney disease concerns
Commence empirical therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily and arrange outpatient follow-up at the haematology day unit in 48 hours
Perform bilateral lower limb compression Doppler ultrasound as initial test and treat only if a deep vein thrombosis is identified on the affected operative limb

subtopic_detail: SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting after SAH
stem:
A 58-year-old woman is on day 7 after surgical clipping of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm following a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Her serum sodium has fallen from 138 to 124 mmol/L over the past 24 hours. She is mildly drowsy. There has been no new neurological deficit on examination this morning.

Nursing observation shows polyuria of 4 litres over the previous 24 hours. On bedside review her mucous membranes are dry, jugular venous pressure is not visible, and capillary return is two seconds. Her body weight has fallen from 68 kg yesterday to 66 kg today. She is on regular enteral feeds via nasogastric tube providing 1500 mL daily and intravenous 0.9 percent saline at 80 mL/hour. She has had no vomiting and no diarrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 100, blood pressure 110/65, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: serum sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 258 mosm/kg (275-295), urine sodium 80 mmol/L, urine osmolality 580 mosm/kg, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, weight reduction 2 kg over 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluid restrict to 800 mL daily, withhold intravenous saline, and arrange demeclocycline 600 mg twice daily for refractory disease over the next 48 hours
Administer 3 percent hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus then continuous infusion at 50 mL/hour and aim for a sodium rise of 10 mmol/L over the next 12 hours
0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour then 200 mL/hour, target sodium rise of 6 to 8 mmol/L over 24 hours, salt tablets 6 g daily if hyponatraemia persists
Demeclocycline 600 mg twice daily as a vasopressin receptor antagonist to allow free water excretion and restore serum sodium gradually toward normal range
Tolvaptan 15 mg daily as a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist with strict fluid restriction to 1 litre per day and daily sodium monitoring on the ward

subtopic_detail: Stanford type A aortic dissection acute management
stem:
A 58-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension presents to a metropolitan emergency department with sudden severe central chest pain radiating to the interscapular region. The pain reached maximum intensity within seconds and has been steady for two hours.

On examination he is in distress. There is a difference between his blood pressure measurements in the right arm and left arm of 40 mmHg. He has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. The chest is clear and the heart sounds are otherwise normal. Chest radiograph demonstrates a widened mediastinum measuring 9 cm. CT angiogram of the aorta has confirmed a Stanford type A dissection extending from the aortic root through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta. There is no malperfusion of major branch vessels reported. The cardiothoracic team are aware.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure right arm 180/100, blood pressure left arm 140/85, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG sinus rhythm without ST changes, troponin within normal limits, chest radiograph widened mediastinum, CT angiogram Stanford type A dissection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting systolic blood pressure below 120 and admit to coronary care for ongoing medical management with antihypertensive review
Aspirin 300 mg, clopidogrel 600 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, and admit to coronary care for management of likely non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
Intravenous labetalol with intravenous nitroprusside as second-line vasodilator and book elective cardiothoracic surgery in 24 to 48 hours after optimisation
Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting heart rate below 60 and systolic blood pressure below 120, opioid analgesia, and immediate cardiothoracic surgery referral for emergency repair
Therapeutic heparin infusion and admit to intensive care for monitoring of haemodynamics and trends in renal function and creatinine over 24 hours

stem:
A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of erythema and severe pain in the left thigh after a minor garden scratch. He describes the pain as far worse than the appearance suggests and is unable to bear weight on the affected leg.

On examination he is septic-appearing but alert. The left thigh shows ill-defined erythema extending from the knee to the upper thigh with marked tenderness but no obvious blistering, no clear demarcation, and no crepitus on palpation. The skin surface looks deceptively mild compared with the pain. The general surgical registrar reviews and is reluctant to operate on grounds of insufficient skin signs, suggesting observation and reassessment in 6 hours with empirical antibiotics. The microbiology registrar has been called by the team.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 110, blood pressure 130/80, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: white cells 19.0 x10^9/L (4-11), haemoglobin 132 g/L (130-180), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 14 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L (<5), lactate 2.8 mmol/L, LRINEC score 8 (CRP 4 + WCC 1 + Hb 0 + Na 2 + creatinine 0 + glucose 1)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and observe with reassessment of the leg appearance and inflammatory markers in six hours of close monitoring
MRI lower limb with contrast to confirm necrotising fasciitis based on fascial enhancement and fluid collections before booking the operating theatre
Punch biopsy of skin sent for frozen section histopathology to confirm fascial necrosis before surgical decision-making is made by the consultant
Bedside ultrasound looking for fascial thickening and subcutaneous fluid then targeted incisional biopsy if those features are seen on the ultrasound
Urgent operating theatre for surgical exploration and aggressive debridement with intravenous meropenem, clindamycin, and vancomycin broad spectrum cover

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia in CKD with competing guideline cutoffs
stem:
A 68-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (baseline eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m^2) presents to the emergency department with worsening fatigue and palpitations. He takes perindopril 8 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, and metformin 500 mg BD, all unchanged for 6 months. His last potassium 4 weeks ago was 5.1 mmol/L. The treating intern has already given him 10 mL of 10 per cent calcium gluconate IV and salbutamol 20 mg via nebuliser, with a repeat ECG pending and a venous gas drawn.

The man is alert, has chest discomfort rated 3 out of 10, and has had no syncope. He has had no missed dialysis (he is pre-dialysis under the renal team and is on a low-potassium diet).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56 bpm regular, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); sodium 138; bicarbonate 16; eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m^2; creatinine 280 micromol/L (baseline 220); pH 7.28 on VBG; ECG sinus bradycardia 54 bpm with tall peaked T waves V2-V5, PR interval 220 ms, QRS 110 ms (was 90 ms at baseline)
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BD

lead_in: Following the initial calcium and salbutamol, what is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50 per cent dextrose over 20 minutes with paired blood glucose at 30 and 60 minutes, repeat ECG, and concurrently contact the nephrology team for emergency haemodialysis
Commence intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 60 minutes with paired blood gas at 30 and 60 minutes, monitor calcium and sodium, and recheck potassium at 60 minutes
Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Resonium) 30 g orally now and 15 g 4-hourly with sorbitol, with repeat potassium at 6 hours and rectal Resonium if the patient cannot tolerate oral
Cease perindopril and spironolactone, repeat potassium at 6 hours, ensure low-potassium diet, and arrange outpatient nephrology review within 1 week
Repeat the calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 per cent IV over 10 minutes, repeat the salbutamol 20 mg nebuliser, and re-check ECG and potassium in 30 minutes before further escalation
